item.title: Kubernetes, mark II? Why Google’s giving away gVisor, a code sandbox used by Anthropic and OpenAI
item.dc:creator: Paul Sawers
item.description:
Google wants to emulate one of its biggest ever open-source success stories, donating three core AI agent infrastructure projects to

The post Kubernetes, mark II? Why Google’s giving away gVisor, a code sandbox used by Anthropic and OpenAI appeared first on The New Stack.
item.content:encoded:
Google wants to emulate one of its biggest ever open-source success stories, donating three core AI agent infrastructure projects to a neutral foundation in the hope they become industry standards, just as Kubernetes did for containers.

In a blog post published on Thursday, Drew Bradstock, VP of product management, Kubernetes and orchestration at Google, confirmed that the company is donating gVisor, Agent Substrate, and OpenRL to the Cloud Native Computing Foundation (CNCF).

The move comes amid growing concerns about the security of autonomous AI agents, particularly their ability to execute code and interact with external systems. In July, models undergoing a cybersecurity evaluation at OpenAI escaped their restricted environment and breached Hugging Face’s production infrastructure, highlighting the challenges of keeping increasingly capable agents contained.

“We believe that these donations will accelerate the development and adoption of agentic workloads through these projects similarly to what we saw with Kubernetes.”

Bradstock, for his part, argues that addressing such security risks, while making agents more economical to run and train, requires closer cooperation across the various facets of the underlying software and hardware infrastructure. And he believes that putting its technologies under neutral governance could encourage the kind of industry-wide participation that helped Kubernetes become ubiquitous.

“We believe that these donations will accelerate the development and adoption of agentic workloads through these projects similarly to what we saw with Kubernetes,” Bradstock writes.

Why Google’s giving away gVisor

By way of a brief recap, Google open-sourced gVisor in 2018 to improve container security. As The New Stack explained later that year, the technology uses a lightweight kernel running in user space to intercept application system calls, providing an additional layer of isolation between containers and the underlying host operating system. This makes it particularly useful for running untrusted code, including code generated by AI agents.

The technology is used by major AI companies, including Anthropic, which runs code generated by Claude inside gVisor containers on its web platform; and OpenAI, which uses it to isolate code execution. In a security report published just on Wednesday, OpenAI cited sandboxes such as gVisor and Firecracker as important for limiting the damage from exploited Linux kernel vulnerabilities.

The donation itself has been in the works for several weeks. The CNCF accepted gVisor’s application in late September, with Google publicly announcing its plans a few days later. The project’s onboarding process began last week, ahead of Thursday’s broader announcement incorporating all three projects.

In its original October announcement, gVisor contributors and Google software engineers Etienne Perot and Jing Chen sought to reassure users that the company remained committed to the technology. With demand for affordable, secure sandboxes growing, they argued that independent governance could encourage wider participation and adoption, both within Google and beyond.

“We (the gVisor contributors at Google) have been pushing for this move internally with the expectation that this will accelerate gVisor’s growth and adoption both within and outside of Google, in a similar manner as what has happened with Kubernetes,” they wrote at the time.

“We have been pushing for this move internally with the expectation that this will accelerate gVisor’s growth and adoption both within and outside of Google.”

Agent Substrate addresses a different challenge: how to run large numbers of autonomous agents without wasting computing resources while they sit idle. As The New Stack reported in July, the project introduces an additional runtime layer on top of Kubernetes, allowing agents to be suspended when inactive and resumed when needed, without repeatedly creating and destroying Kubernetes Pods. It does this by separating an agent’s persistent state from the computing resources executing it, with gVisor providing one of the available options for securely isolating that execution.

As part of the announcement this week, Google officially released Agent Substrate 1.0 and made it generally available on Google Kubernetes Engine (GKE).

OpenRL, meanwhile, focuses on reinforcement learning, allowing developers to fine-tune AI models on their own Kubernetes infrastructure. Publicly introduced in June, the project coordinates the training and evaluation processes used to improve models. It also integrates with Agent Substrate, allowing training exercises to run inside isolated environments that can be secured using gVisor.

Collectively, the three projects address the execution, security and training requirements of autonomous AI agents.

Going vendor neutral

The move to CNCF governance should also change how gVisor is developed and maintained. In their October announcement, Perot and Chen outlined plans to move the project’s development and testing infrastructure outside Google, give external maintainers permission to merge code, and introduce a governance model that prevents any single company from exercising unilateral control.

Notably, in the project’s CNCF application submitted through GitHub in September, Perot identified a divide among gVisor’s existing adopters. At one end are major technology companies such as Anthropic and OpenAI, which can invest in adapting the technology to their needs; at the other are specialist startups whose businesses depend heavily on secure code execution. The opportunity, Perot suggested, lies in reaching the much broader market between those two camps.

Such companies “don’t have the resources to invest specifically into security but would happily adopt an off-the-shelf, widely-available sandboxing runtime,” Perot wrote in the application.

There’s also the question of why more cloud providers haven’t integrated gVisor into their commercial offerings. In their October announcement, Perot and Chen noted that Google, DigitalOcean and Modal were among the few providers selling general-purpose computing services powered by gVisor, despite evidence that customers were already installing the technology themselves on competing cloud platforms. The engineers suggested that concerns about Google’s control of the project could explain the discrepancy.

“The remaining explanation of the lack of direct integration is likely the project’s (pre-donation) governance risk,” they wrote.

But perhaps the most interesting obstacle concerns the Linux kernel itself. Google and other companies using gVisor maintain their own kernel modifications to improve its performance, particularly for I/O-intensive applications. Those improvements aren’t universally available, potentially leaving other users with slower execution environments.

Bradstock attributes the difficulty in getting those improvements incorporated into the mainline Linux kernel to gVisor’s hitherto Google-centric credentials.

“Upstream Linux maintainers declined to merge them while the project was owned by a single vendor.”

“Upstream Linux maintainers declined to merge them while the project was owned by a single vendor,” Bradstock writes.

There is also documented resistance to at least one earlier gVisor-related kernel proposal on technical grounds. As LWN reported in 2022, Linux kernel maintainers raised security and design concerns about a proposed performance improvement, including questions about its usefulness beyond gVisor.

While such interactions don’t focus on Google’s ownership as a reason for the objections, it’s clear that moving to CNCF governance should go some distance toward addressing concerns about single-vendor control.

And for Google, that effort now extends beyond gVisor. With Agent Substrate and OpenRL also moving to the CNCF, the company is hoping to establish a common foundation for autonomous agents.

“Vendor-neutral ownership lets cloud providers, hardware vendors, and independent software companies participate in the future growth of agentic workloads equally,” Bradstock writes.

The post Kubernetes, mark II? Why Google’s giving away gVisor, a code sandbox used by Anthropic and OpenAI appeared first on The New Stack.
The sandbox heads to the CNCF alongside Agent Substrate and OpenRL, as Google bets neutral governance can make its AI agent stack an industry standard.

item.title: HumanLayer just got acquired by Factory. But it gave users a way out first.
item.dc:creator: Amanda Caswell
item.description:
Factory has acquired HumanLayer, its third AI coding startup in less than a month, as it works to fold more

The post HumanLayer just got acquired by Factory. But it gave users a way out first. appeared first on The New Stack.
item.content:encoded:
Factory has acquired HumanLayer, its third AI coding startup in less than a month, as it works to fold more of the software engineering lifecycle into a single autonomous platform. The deal deepens Factory’s bench, but it also leaves existing HumanLayer users weighing what to do with the tools they already depend on.

Announced Wednesday, the acquisition brings HumanLayer founders Dex Horthy and Kyle Mistele to Factory, along with technology for coordinating multiple coding agents and collaborating on their work. It arrives as demand for agentic coding tools climbs at a pace few enterprise products ever see, pushing the companies building them to consolidate fast.

“It arrives as demand for agentic coding tools climbs at a pace few enterprise products ever see…”

Factory co-founder and CEO Matan Grinberg welcomes the pair on X, writing that he has “been a huge fan of @dexhorthy and @0xblacklight for a while now,” and calling them two of the most ambitious polymaths he has met.

What happens to users

The founders write in their announcement that Factory will “also be refunding paying customers for the last several months,” though neither company has set a shutdown date for HumanLayer’s hosted service or said which features will carry over.

For users who would rather not migrate, HumanLayer open-sourced its core software under Apache 2.0 on October 23, an escape hatch that still comes with caveats. Some processes require third-party API keys even when those integrations go unused, a rough edge the company says it is working to remove as it makes the software easier to deploy on its own.

Three deals, four weeks

HumanLayer caps a quick run of deals that map Factory’s priorities. On October 9, Factory acquired Mentlio, a Y Combinator startup focused on making coding agents more cost-efficient through model routing, context compression and spending analysis.

Three weeks later, on October 30, it acquired Typedef, which builds tools for understanding the relationships across data models, pipelines and dashboards, technology Factory plans to point at enterprise data migrations and refactoring.

HumanLayer brings collaboration to that mix, with multiplayer tasks, shared editing of agent-generated plans and documents, and live streaming of code changes during agent sessions. Factory says those capabilities will begin arriving over the coming weeks without naming specific release dates, and it has not disclosed the purchase price for any of the three deals.

Inside Factory’s agent playbook

Factory’s coding agents, known as Droids, handle everything from planning and writing code to testing and maintenance. HumanLayer’s founders have focused on what happens when teams run multiple coding agents at once, including managing context, coordinating tasks, and reviewing results.

Factory’s coding agents, known as Droids, handle everything from planning and writing code to testing and maintenance.

Horthy and Mistele also helped popularize the Research/Plan/Implement workflow, which breaks coding tasks into separate stages. Their work fits Factory’s effort to bring more of the development process into one platform. Mentlio helps control agent costs, Typedef adds enterprise data capabilities, and HumanLayer brings tools for collaboration.

The standalone question

But HumanLayer users still don’t know whether the hosted service will continue beyond the transition, what they’ll pay if they move to Factory, or which features they’ll be able to keep. The open-source version gives them another option, although they’ll have to host and maintain it themselves. For now, it’s unclear how much of HumanLayer will remain available as a standalone product.

“HumanLayer users still don’t know whether the hosted service will continue beyond the transition, what they’ll pay if they move to Factory, or which features they’ll be able to keep.”

Factory has acquired HumanLayer, its third AI coding startup in a month, leaving users to migrate, pay up, or self-host the open source version.

item.title: OpenAI’s new GPT-6 Cyber is better at hacking and better at staying in its lane
item.dc:creator: Frederic Lardinois
item.description:
OpenAI on Thursday launched GPT-6 Cyber, the latest release in its series of cybersecurity-focused models. The company ranks GPT-6 Cyber’s ability

The post OpenAI’s new GPT-6 Cyber is better at hacking and better at staying in its lane appeared first on The New Stack.
item.content:encoded:
OpenAI on Thursday launched GPT-6 Cyber, the latest release in its series of cybersecurity-focused models.

The company ranks GPT-6 Cyber’s ability to identify vulnerabilities and develop exploits as ‘critical,’ up from ‘high’ for its predecessor. Just like with previous Cyber models, GPT-6 Cyber will not be available to all developers but only to “a select group of approved Daybreak Red customers,” OpenAI says.

Daybreak Red access only

Daybreak is OpenAI’s program for security teams and researchers, with Daybreak Red being a subsection for authorized red teaming, penetration testing, and exploit validation (as opposed to Daybreak Blue, its defensive counterpart).

Over time, OpenAI plans to open the model to all Daybreak Red users.

OpenAI also notes that it plans to expand the Daybreak program to more security researchers, organizations, and, critically, open source maintainers. “It is clear that we have a limited window to use frontier models to secure software⁠,” OpenAI writes. It notes that its own researchers used the new model to uncover flaws and build exploits in Firefox and the Linux kernel, while security teams at Cisco and CodeRabbit already rely on it for code review and vulnerability hunting.

Built on GPT-6 Astra

OpenAI says the new model is “a major leap in security research.”

GPT-6 Cyber is a specialized version of GPT-6 Astra. OpenAI says it used reinforcement learning to train the model to reproduce crashes, develop exploits, and find vulnerabilities in code, while also rewarding it for staying within the user’s authorized scope and reducing unnecessary refusals.

Benchmarks

On ExploitGym, which tests whether models can exploit a specified vulnerability on a remote target, GPT-6 Cyber scores 48.5%, compared with GPT-5.6 Cyber’s 32.1%, OpenAI says.

For finding vulnerabilities in web applications without access to their source code, the new model scores 40.3%, compared with 32% for GPT-6 Astra (which is widely available).

On ExploitBench, which tests exploit development using known vulnerabilities, OpenAI reports a 100% mean capability score. The company notes, though, that the benchmark includes vulnerabilities dating back to 2023 and those examples may have appeared in training data, potentially inflating the results.

Staying within its authorized scope

With this announcement, the company also introduced RemoteExploitBench, a benchmark that asks models to exploit known vulnerabilities in applications like GitLab, PostgreSQL, and Jenkins in a controlled environment.

An agent that’s this willing to exploit systems can also wander outside its assigned task and go after services it was never meant to touch, OpenAI notes.

It looks like GPT-6 Cyber is far better at staying in bounds than its predecessors, though.

OpenAI tests for this with ExploitGym Honeypot, a new test it built with the Hugging Face incident in mind. This test gives the model a difficult exploitation task inside a sandbox that also includes helper services (think a package registry or object storage), which OpenAI deliberately left easy to break into. Hacking them would be a shortcut to the flag the model is after, but they’re outside the scope of the task, and the model has to work that out on its own.

Without a deployment safety prompt, GPT-6 Cyber left those services alone in 99.93% of tests. With the prompt, it never touched them.

Under the same conditions, GPT-5.6 Cyber went after those services in 5.51% of runs, according to the system card, and the general-purpose GPT-5.6 Sol did so in almost half of them. GPT-6 Astra, the model GPT-6 Cyber is based on, never took the bait.

What’s maybe just as important, though, is that the new model is far more aligned than previous versions. GPT‑6 Cyber, OpenAI says, stayed away from “out-of-scope services” in 99.93% of tests run without its deployment safety prompt and in all of them when the prompt was in place.

“This improvement in alignment reflects dedicated training to stay within authorized scope, respect restrictions, and report results accurately,” OpenAI writes.

The post OpenAI’s new GPT-6 Cyber is better at hacking and better at staying in its lane appeared first on The New Stack.
OpenAI’s GPT-6 Cyber is rated critical for exploit work and is far better at staying in scope. For now, only select Daybreak Red customers get access.

item.title: Together AI let coding agents rewrite its GPU code. Then it kept humans on the deploy button.
item.dc:creator: Amanda Caswell
item.description:
Together AI is putting AI coding agents to work on the GPU code that runs its inference infrastructure, automating performance

The post Together AI let coding agents rewrite its GPU code. Then it kept humans on the deploy button. appeared first on The New Stack.
item.content:encoded:
Together AI is putting AI coding agents to work on the GPU code that runs its inference infrastructure, automating performance tuning that used to take engineers days or weeks of manual work.

The company unveiled Together Compiler on Wednesday, a system that generates, tests, and improves GPU kernels without an engineer directing each experiment, and Together AI says it can deliver gains overnight. The process runs without a person steering each step, but it doesn’t ship anything on its own.

Asked how much people remain in the loop, Together AI tells The New Stack, “The optimization loop is autonomous,” adding that “the final evaluations and deployment process are automatic but must be kicked off by a human, who reviews the changes before deploying to production.”

“The optimization loop is autonomous. The final evaluations and deployment process … must be kicked off by a human, who reviews the changes before deploying to production.”

Why GPU kernels fall behind

New AI models arrive so frequently that keeping inference infrastructure optimized has become a challenge. Each model has different requirements, and GPU code tuned for one workload may not perform nearly as well on another.

Together AI says 80% of OpenRouter traffic now comes from models released within the past three months. That leaves engineers constantly adjusting code to keep up; now Together Compiler automates much of that work.

Multiple coding agents run experiments simultaneously, writing and testing GPU kernels while sharing results to help guide the next round of improvements.

Faster testing, more experiments

The company has also found a way to speed up testing. Instead of restarting an inference engine every time an agent changes the code, Together Compiler keeps the engine running and loads new code. According to Together AI, this cuts initialization time from roughly 467 seconds to just nine seconds.

Instead of restarting an inference engine every time an agent changes the code, Together Compiler keeps the engine running and loads new code.

Reading the 252x claim

Together AI says its compiler can run 252 times as many optimization experiments as existing agent-based systems. The company tells The New Stack that it used Apple’s RSI Inference Bench harness as its baseline, comparing both systems on the same inference workload and hardware, with only the optimization approach changing.

The 252x figure refers to the number of experiments Together Compiler can run compared with Apple’s system, not how much faster the AI models themselves perform.

The company separately reports inference throughput improvements of up to 2.6x compared with published benchmark configurations. Those gains depend on the model and hardware, and the results haven’t been independently verified.

More experiments give Together Compiler more chances to find improvements. And because each test takes less time, the agents can do overnight what might otherwise take engineers weeks of manual tuning.

Better performance, same cost

Faster inference doesn’t necessarily mean lower prices. Asked whether the performance gains would translate into customer savings or primarily improve its own infrastructure efficiency, Together AI tells The New Stack, “Together Compiler improves Together AI’s infrastructure efficiency. For the same dollar cost, customers will get better performance.”

“For the same dollar cost, customers will get better performance.”

Developers may get more work out of the same GPUs, but that doesn’t always mean lower per-token prices. The company tells The New Stack that customers will get better performance for the same cost, rather than a price reduction.

Together AI says its compiler is already serving trillions of tokens daily. It’s another sign that coding agents are moving beyond writing application code and into GPU performance optimization, with engineers reviewing work that agents can now complete overnight.

The post Together AI let coding agents rewrite its GPU code. Then it kept humans on the deploy button. appeared first on The New Stack.
Together AI’s new Together Compiler lets AI coding agents tune GPU kernels overnight, but engineers still approve changes before they reach production.

item.title: Raindrop simulates your agent’s world to catch what your changes break
item.dc:creator: Frederic Lardinois
item.description:
Raindrop wants developers to know what else will change when they edit an agent’s prompt, swap its model, or give

The post Raindrop simulates your agent’s world to catch what your changes break appeared first on The New Stack.
item.content:encoded:
Raindrop wants developers to know what else will change when they edit an agent’s prompt, swap its model, or give it a new tool.

The company, which started out as a monitoring startup for agents (“Sentry for agents” was its early motto), is making its Simulations platform available in public beta on Thursday.

An agent’s prompt can depend on feature flags, account details, and the user’s plan, says Ben Hylak, Raindrop’s co-founder and CTO.

“You have to put the agent in motion in order to really evaluate it,” he says.

With Simulations, Raindrop reconstructs an agent’s production environment, including its tools, APIs, and databases, so developers can see how a change affects its behavior before shipping it, the company says. That change could be a model swap, a prompt edit, or a new tool — any of which could change an agent’s behavior in production.

“Every time agents run, they go different paths.” — Raindrop CTO Ben Hylak.

Hylak argues that predefined tests and evals can miss failures developers didn’t anticipate, especially as agents take on more consequential work.

“Every time agents run, they go different paths,” Hylak says.

Rebuilding the environment

Raindrop describes its simulation environment as a set of stateful synthetic services that the customer’s real agent code runs against. It uses production traces to reconstruct the services the agent interacts with, filling gaps with generated data.

The agent runs its real prompts, models, and agent loop in an isolated sandbox without access to production services or credentials, according to Raindrop. For each tool call, Raindrop generates a response grounded in production traces, validates it against the types the code expects, and keeps the simulated environment consistent throughout the run.

Running the test against live services wouldn’t recreate the original conditions, either, Hylak says.

“The state of production has changed since you were running that agent,” he says.

Hylak says Raindrop sets up the agent harness and test environment automatically, using sandboxes both to build and run the simulations. The agent under test may also create sandboxes of its own.

“It’s like sandboxes all the way down,” he says.

Hylak says Raindrop runs its production issue detection over the simulations to find failures and unexpected changes in behavior. The company is looking for failures a developer didn’t anticipate, as well as checking the scenarios the developer already wrote down.

Filling in missing data

Simulating the environment is one thing, but the agents also need data to work with. A prompt edit or model swap can reuse context from earlier runs, Hylak says. Adding a Salesforce or HubSpot tool is harder because Raindrop may never have seen the data that it returns.

Raindrop can generate synthetic data to fill in the holes, but Hylak says, “We know that that will be a less faithful simulation than the real world.”

To give its users confidence in those simulations, Raindrop gives them a simulation fidelity score and flags what’s lowering it, Hylak says. The score estimates how closely the test reflects production. Customers can then add a file or connect a data source through the Model Context Protocol and rerun the test under more realistic conditions.

A missing feature-flag value can also leave the simulator without information that shaped the original prompt. Hylak says Raindrop can suggest pull requests that improve the agent’s telemetry so that context gets recorded.

Models can often pick up on inconsistencies in synthetic data and realize they’re being tested, Hylak says. That can change their behavior during the test. The team tries to measure this testing awareness as part of its simulations.

To account for normal variation between runs, Raindrop also runs multiple simulations and compares the findings with production history, Hylak says.

Testing different agents

OpenAI already uses production conversations to test candidate models, including coding agents whose tools are simulated using historical repository state and recorded tool interactions. Sierra, meanwhile, automatically generates simulation suites for agents on its platform using standard operating procedures, knowledge bases, historical coaching transcripts, and conversation flows.

Hylak says Raindrop is building for customers’ own agents, across different frameworks and codebases, with results delivered as part of the pull request. During early access, the team had to get the simulations working with agents embedded in large enterprise codebases.

During early access, customers and Raindrop’s own team ran more than 33,000 simulations across more than 1,700 pull requests, according to the company.

OpenAI’s account of the Hugging Face incident describes agents exploiting interconnected systems during cybersecurity evaluations with reduced safeguards. More recently, it documented internal coding agents weakening monitoring while carrying out software changes.

Raindrop first announced Simulations in September, alongside a Series A that brought its total funding to $50 million.

Pricing will be based on pull requests, Hylak says, with charges for reconstructing the environment and running the simulations. The agent’s own model usage is initially billed through Raindrop as well, so the bill will depend in part on how long the agent runs.

The post Raindrop simulates your agent’s world to catch what your changes break appeared first on The New Stack.
Raindrop’s Simulations, now in public beta, rebuilds an AI agent’s production environment so developers can test prompt edits, model swaps, and new tools.

item.title: Groundcover automates Kubernetes sizing. Engineers set the bounds.
item.dc:creator: Meredith Shubel
item.description:
On Tuesday, groundcover launched Autonomous Infrastructure in beta to continuously adjust CPU and memory requests for Kubernetes (K8s) Deployments based

The post Groundcover automates Kubernetes sizing. Engineers set the bounds. appeared first on The New Stack.
item.content:encoded:
On Tuesday, groundcover launched Autonomous Infrastructure in beta to continuously adjust CPU and memory requests for Kubernetes (K8s) Deployments based on production data. 

Built on technology from Wand, the K8s resource optimization platform groundcover acquired in September, the beta uses data already collected from groundcover’s eBPF sensor to inform resource allocation decisions, while giving engineers a direct view into how those decisions could affect infrastructure costs and workload performance. 

Shahar Azulay, CEO and co-founder of groundcover, tells The New Stack about the balance the company is trying to get right: “The goal isn’t simply to reduce resource requests as much as possible. It’s to find the right balance between efficiency and stability across the entire environment.” 

That can mean reducing requests for workloads consuming far less than they’ve been allocated, but it can also mean increasing requests when a workload needs additional resources to operate reliably. The objective is not simply a smaller infrastructure footprint. It’s an environment that continuously receives the resources it needs, without paying for capacity it doesn’t.

How to get there? Azulay says teams need “a continuous feedback loop that uses real production telemetry to identify when workloads are over- or under-provisioned and safely adjust them.” 

Does nobody know a good way to right-size K8s workloads?

It’s not for lack of trying. There are already a lot of different ways to tackle the burden of right-sizing K8s workloads. 

For example, scheduled rightsizing applies changes at chosen intervals, so it may not respond between scheduled updates. In-place resizing can change resources on running pods, although some changes require container restarts. Automated tools can also generate and apply recommendations within policies engineers set. 

When asked why he thinks K8s rightsizing continues to trip people up, Azulay tells The New Stack the challenge lies in striking the right balance between cost efficiency and application stability: 

“Resource requests are typically set at deployment time, when teams are making their best estimates before a workload has experienced real-world production traffic,” he explains. “The challenge is that workloads are constantly changing, but resource configurations often aren’t.” 

“The challenge is that workloads are constantly changing, but resource configurations often aren’t.”

After initial deployment, teams may simply let sleeping workloads lie, i.e., they don’t revisit original resource requests for reconfiguration. While workloads may keep spinning along just fine, this approach means teams risk unknowingly leaving them over- or under-provisioned—with costly consequences. 

For organizations running hundreds or thousands of workloads, keeping those configurations accurate becomes an ongoing engineering task. Teams must analyze utilization, identify opportunities, test new settings, and revisit them as traffic and application behavior change. Even with the expertise, they may not have the time to do it continuously.

Azulay describes over-provisioning as “the safer choice because nobody wants to risk performance issues or outages.” But that extra peace of mind can come with unnecessary infrastructure costs; in a 2025 study published in Applied Sciences, researchers found that optimizing K8s resource allocation improved a combined performance-and-cost score by approximately 50% compared to the conventional maximum resource allocation approach. 

Under-provisioning carries different risks. Requests help Kubernetes schedule pods, and CPU requests influence how CPU time is shared under contention; setting them too low can leave workloads short of CPU time. Limits work differently: CPU limits cause throttling, while exceeding a memory limit can trigger an out-of-memory (OOM) kill. Low memory requests can also increase eviction risk when a node is under memory pressure. 

There’s also a relationship between workload requests and the cost of the cluster itself. Node autoscalers such as Karpenter can provision or remove nodes based on the resources workloads request, but they don’t determine whether those requests accurately reflect what each application needs. If workloads consistently request too much, the autoscaler may maintain more capacity than necessary. Right-sizing those requests gives the node autoscaler a more accurate basis for allocating infrastructure.

What if the answer to done-right right-sizing is sitting in your production data? 

Groundcover thinks so. That’s why its new Autonomous Infrastructure draws on the groundcover eBPF sensor, which is already collecting telemetry across applications and infrastructure. The beta uses that production history to recommend CPU and memory requests for Kubernetes Deployments. Brand-new Deployments remain in a learning state until enough data is available. 

But the approach isn’t simply to observe a spike in resource consumption and increase requests afterward. By the time a reactive system responds, the performance impact may already have occurred. Instead, groundcover’s optimization engine analyzes workload behavior over time, including usage patterns and resource contention, to anticipate capacity requirements and prepare workloads for expected changes in demand.

That distinction matters for workloads with recurring traffic spikes. The goal is to have enough resources available when demand arrives, without permanently allocating for peak consumption.

When engineers open the beta, they get a direct view of how much CPU and memory each workload requests versus what it uses, plus the number of under-provisioned workloads and estimated monthly savings if they apply changes. Groundcover’s product page says dollar estimates use default list prices that administrators can adjust with their own prices and discounts. These estimates do not establish that a cloud bill will fall by the same amount; realizing savings also depends on whether freed capacity lets teams reduce billed infrastructure. 

An important part of the experience is that customers can see those opportunities before enabling autonomous optimization. Because groundcover already collects the necessary telemetry, existing customers can evaluate potential savings without deploying a separate monitoring agent or conducting another data-collection exercise. They can inspect recommendations, understand their expected impact, and decide which workloads, if any, to optimize.

Rather than setting resource requests at deployment time and letting them run on autopilot, engineers can use Autonomous Infrastructure to put real-time telemetry to work and continuously adjust resources based on production behavior. And because groundcover already collects the necessary telemetry, teams running a supported sensor version don’t need a separate agent or a new data-collection period for existing Deployments with sufficient history. 

Why the answer lies in the context

When asked how real-time production data can improve K8s right-sizing, Azulay tells The New Stack it comes down to understanding how workloads affect one another in production. 

While some resource optimization tools size each workload on its own, he claims that approach doesn’t tell the whole story.

“Kubernetes workloads don’t operate in isolation. They share nodes, compete for available resources, and can directly affect one another’s performance.”

Instead, to find the optimal balance between efficiency and stability, Azulay says engineers need tools that consider the entire environment: 

“Kubernetes workloads don’t operate in isolation. They share nodes, compete for available resources, and can directly affect one another’s performance.” 

For example, lowering CPU requests changes how a workload shares CPU under contention and can let the scheduler pack more workloads onto a node. A recommendation based only on one workload’s usage can therefore miss contention effects across the node. 

This is one limitation of approaches that rely primarily on historical utilization for each workload. Two applications with similar CPU consumption may require different resource allocations depending on their traffic patterns, neighboring workloads, and the contention they experience. Applying the same sizing formula to both can leave one over-provisioned and the other vulnerable to performance problems.

To right-size each workload without bruising others, Azulay tells The New Stack resource optimization tools must not only evaluate real-time resource consumption against what’s being requested but consider the traffic patterns, workload behavior, and available resources across the node: 

“True optimization requires understanding both individual workload behavior and the broader environment in which those workloads operate.”

Azulay says Autonomous Infrastructure uses that broader context. Leaning on Wand’s optimization engine, the beta uses node-level contention to inform right-sizing recommendations and make adjustments that consider the entire environment. 

“It also looks beyond application containers to account for injected sidecars, such as Istio, Linkerd and Vault agents, which can be overlooked sources of resource waste,” Azulay says. 

The integration with groundcover also connects resource optimization to the observability workflows engineers already use. Rather than receiving an isolated recommendation from a separate optimization tool, engineers can investigate workload behavior using the logs, traces, metrics, and infrastructure context available in the same platform. That helps them understand why a change was recommended and evaluate its impact on the environment.

The result is a connection between observing infrastructure and acting on what the data reveals. Production telemetry informs optimization decisions, and engineers can use that same observability context to understand what happens afterward.

But are engineers ready to automate right-sizing?

Letting a tool like Autonomous Infrastructure take over K8s right-sizing can sound like a convenient solution. As Azulay tells The New Stack, many teams simply don’t get around to reconfiguring resource requests because of time and resource constraints — and engineers aren’t always sure the changes will improve efficiency without impacting stability. 

But that doesn’t necessarily mean engineers are ready to go all in on automated right-sizing, at least for now. In Kube.today’s 2025 community poll on Kubernetes resource management, 56.5% of respondents selected manual tools such as kubectl and dashboards as their primary approach. That result reflects the poll’s respondents, not Kubernetes practitioners as a whole. 

Groundcover’s own research, administered by Atomik Research, underlines engineers’ uncertainty about going fully autonomous. In the survey of 500 U.S. technology professionals, 87% say AI or automation is already integrated into observability workflows, but only one-third (34%) call it “fully operational and trusted.” 

For those hesitant to hand over the reins for resource optimization, groundcover’s beta might offer some relief.

Per groundcover, Autonomous Infrastructure is “opt-in at every level.” By default, automation is off; groundcover’s launch blog describes opting in a cluster and then enabling individual Deployments.

While the beta may use production telemetry to autonomously adjust resource requests, engineers still set the parameters, defining minimum and maximum bounds for CPU and memory requests. The beta changes requests only, leaving limits unchanged. A declared limit caps the recommendation; a workload constrained by that limit appears as “Bounded.” Groundcover says every policy change is versioned and an audit log records who assigned each workload to a policy and when. A resource used by an HPA or KEDA utilization-based autoscaler is left unchanged. The beta uses in-place resizing when possible and falls back to a rollout when necessary. 

For engineers who may be wary of giving a resource optimization tool full access to decide and execute K8s right-sizing, these constraints can ease the transition. Plus, they can easily keep a pulse on what the beta is doing, with groundcover’s view showing how many workloads are managed autonomously in each cluster and namespace. 

“…engineers aren’t being asked to trust a black box.”

Perhaps more importantly, engineers aren’t being asked to trust a black box. They can review the reasoning behind recommendations, inspect the expected effects, and choose precisely where to enable autonomous changes. The automation is designed to remain understandable and reversible.

Who will get right-sizing right?

Groundcover says the Autonomous Infrastructure beta is available at no additional cost to its customers running the groundcover sensor on Kubernetes, with a supported sensor version required. The beta covers Deployments and their sidecars; support for other workload kinds is on the roadmap. The company is inviting design partners and plans demonstrations at booth #111 during KubeCon + CloudNativeCon North America, Nov. 9–12, 2026, in Salt Lake City. 

The question for the next generation of Kubernetes optimization tools may be less about how aggressively they can reduce resource requests and more about how intelligently they can manage them. That means anticipating demand, accounting for contention across the environment, and making changes engineers can understand and trust.

For groundcover, bringing optimization into the same platform that collects and analyzes production telemetry is a step toward that model: infrastructure that doesn’t just report what’s happening, but uses that understanding to continuously improve how it runs.

Groundcover’s new beta right-sizes Kubernetes workloads from eBPF telemetry. But engineers still decide where, and how far, the automation can go.

item.title: AI failures threaten incident management: Here are 4 ways to avoid them.
item.dc:creator: João Freitas
item.description:
AI is becoming woven into the fabric of digital operations and incident management. On the one hand, AI can detect,

The post AI failures threaten incident management: Here are 4 ways to avoid them. appeared first on The New Stack.
item.content:encoded:
AI is becoming woven into the fabric of digital operations and incident management. On the one hand, AI can detect, triage, and remediate incidents faster, improve coordination between teams, prevent repeat incidents, and drive process redesign. In some organizations, AI is already moving beyond assisting teams to acting on their behalf, as agents pave the way for autonomous digital operations.

On the other hand, greater autonomy also introduces greater risk. Unlike traditional software systems, AI-powered incident management tools and agents fail in ways that traditional ITOps and DevOps teams aren’t used to – less predictable and harder to detect. AI has specific failure modes, including hallucinations, groundedness issues, model drift, guardrail violations, or poor tool selection. When these incidents happen, there is often no big-bang failure to set alarm bells ringing. Instead, errors cascade across services into major issues, especially in multi-agent systems.

“When these incidents happen, there is often no big-bang failure to set alarm bells ringing. Instead, errors cascade across services into major issues.”

The good news is that organizations can mitigate these risks by focusing on four key areas.

1. Deploy guardrails

    No two organizations are at the same level of maturity when it comes to AI integration. Some are in the adoption and experimentation phase, while others are building ultra-complex workflows with whole networks of specialized agents. The more autonomy an agent has, the further a single bad decision can travel before anyone notices.

    As organizations’ AI use matures, they need guardrails in place to enforce policy and limit risk. That includes implementing controls to ensure agents stop, self-report, or hand off to a human when they start to drift from their intended behavior. ITOps and engineering teams can then intervene before small problems become significant ones. These controls must contain risk without creating unnecessary friction for engineering teams.

    2. Use AI agents to monitor and respond

    As organizations deploy larger numbers of agents, monitoring their behavior becomes too complex for humans alone. That creates a need for a new layer of oversight in the form of agents designed to monitor other AI systems. By assessing the signals AI systems generate, monitoring agents can identify abnormal behavior and determine when an issue needs to be escalated to a responder. In agentic systems, this responder may not be a human operator, but another AI agent designed for incident mitigation. Almost 70% of incidents stem from changes, so when AI is making changes at machine speed, organizations need to respond at the same pace.

    “Almost 70% of incidents stem from changes, so when AI is making changes at machine speed, organizations need to respond at the same pace.”

    Consider a Site Reliability Engineering (SRE) agent designed to investigate as soon as it detects a system anomaly. By the time an on-call engineer is notified, the SRE agent could be investigating, triaging, and diagnosing. Connecting the agent to code, telemetry, infrastructure, and collaboration tools makes those investigations more accurate. Where an incident is a repeat, the agent could also trigger pre-approved mitigation workflows. That provides a pathway to AI-assisted incident management and, eventually, self-healing agentic systems.

    3. Identify metrics

    To know whether agents are behaving as intended, engineering teams need meaningful ways to measure performance. The relevance of each metric will depend on the AI agent and its associated work. However, in general, important metrics include task success (did the agent accomplish what it was supposed to?), groundedness (whether an agent’s responses are supported by the information given to it, or whether it is hallucinating), latency, tool selection, timeout rates, error rates, retry rates, step efficiency, cost, safety and ethical violations, human escalation rates, and many others. One option for evaluating the performance of AI agents is to create a golden set of expected behaviors (e.g., a set of questions and answers) and ensure that the agent is operating as intended in the cases covered by the golden set.

    4. Build in ongoing evaluation

    Agent performance is not fixed. Behavior can shift if the model behind an agent is updated, and it can drift even when the underlying infrastructure remains healthy. Any decline in performance should be treated as an operational issue, with alerts routed to the right team before a problem escalates.

    Evaluation should happen at two speeds: catching issues near real time and reviewing agent behavior after the fact. Post-incident reviews examine not only what went wrong, but how agents behaved in response. Did they escalate appropriately? Were the right tools selected? Was human intervention required when it should have been? As systems become more autonomous, agent evaluation must become an ongoing discipline.

    Start off small

    AI has the potential to transform incident management, but organizations will only realize that opportunity when they can trust their AI agents. Building that trust starts with low-risk use cases such as triage and diagnosis, before gradually automating more of the incident lifecycle.

    “AI has the potential to transform incident management, but organizations will only realize that opportunity when they can trust their AI agents.”

    Trust also comes from putting the right guardrails, monitoring, and evaluation processes in place. While human oversight will remain essential for complex incidents, the long-term direction is clear: engineers and AI agents will increasingly work together to resolve issues.

Autonomous AI brings new failure modes to digital operations. Explore 4 ways to implement guardrails, monitor agents, and build trust.

item.title: Postcards from tomorrow: Powering the agentic era through open source
item.dc:creator: Lachlan Evenson
item.description:
When organizations across the industry first adopted generative AI, most consumed it through a hosted API, but open-weight models are

The post Postcards from tomorrow: Powering the agentic era through open source appeared first on The New Stack.
item.content:encoded:
When organizations across the industry first adopted generative AI, most consumed it through a hosted API, but open-weight models are changing that. Models like the Qwen family and GLM-5 are published on model registries like Hugging Face, many under Apache 2.0 licensing, and load directly into open-source serving engines like vLLM and SGLang.

“For a growing set of workloads, that gap is small enough that the model is no longer the main constraint.”

Closed models pulled further ahead in 2025, but not by much. The Stanford AI Index 2026 put the top closed model’s lead over the top open model on the Arena leaderboard at 3.3% as of March 2026. For a growing set of workloads, that gap is small enough that the model is no longer the main constraint.

KubeCon + CloudNativeCon is taking place in Salt Lake City from November 9 to 12. Register now!

Serving a downloaded model is the easy part; the value comes from changing it: fine-tuning on your own data or applying reinforcement learning (RL) against your own tasks, then putting the improved version back into service. That learning loop is where most of the cost and infrastructure complexity sits.

Consider an internal coding agent that a platform team builds to fix failing CI builds that runs on an open-weight model pulled from Hugging Face. When a build fails, the agent clones the repository into a sandbox, reads the logs, writes a patch, and runs the tests. Every attempt produces a trajectory, the record of a single run, with a clean reward signal, because the tests either pass or they don’t.

Those trajectories feed the learning loop. On a schedule, the team fine-tunes the model on successful fixes or runs an RL job against the reward, then evaluates the new checkpoint and rolls it out behind the existing endpoint. Over time, the model learns how the team’s codebase breaks and how it gets fixed. That one workflow combines three workload types, and each stresses a platform differently.

Where a learning loop gets hard

  1. Three workloads, three platforms? 
    Inference needs long-running replicas that scale with traffic and start quickly. Fine-tuning and RL jobs are close to the opposite: gang-scheduled across GPUs and run to completion. Agents need short-lived execution environments that spin up fast. Teams that stand up separate infrastructure for each end up with idle GPUs in one place and queued jobs in another, and every handoff adds cost.
  2. Untrusted code at high density
    Agents execute code the model wrote seconds earlier, and a shared kernel is a thin boundary. The CI agent from our example also spends most of its life waiting on a model response or a test run. Giving each agent a dedicated, always-on pod makes isolation expensive, so teams trade security for density.
  3. Scattered capacity and slow starts
    Teams add GPUs incrementally, across regions, and sometimes on hardware they already own on-premises. A training job may fit on capacity that exists but sits outside the cluster, and when inference scales out, each new replica has to load tens of gigabytes of weights before it serves a single request.

One control plane for the whole loop

Rather than building a separate platform for each stage, treat the learning loop as a standard cloud native systems problem. Kubernetes already reconciles declared state and schedules work. The job is now to extend those primitives to models, agents, and accelerators, giving the pattern three layers on a shared control plane.

Model layer: serving and tuning as declarative workloads

The model layer covers serving, fine-tuning, and evaluation. Several open-source projects work here, including KServe, llm-d and the Kubernetes AI Toolchain Operator (KAITO). KAITO represents a model and its GPU requirements as a custom resource and reconciles that state. A model update becomes a change to desired state, not a script someone has to run.

On the training side, Kueue handles queueing and gang scheduling while KubeRay orchestrates distributed jobs. If you’d rather not assemble those pieces yourself, TauGrid, which Microsoft open-sourced in August 2026, packages them with GPU health monitoring and observability into a single Helm install.

Model streaming helps with cold starts. The Run:ai Model Streamer, supported in vLLM, reads tensors from object storage straight into GPU memory rather than staging them on local disk first, so new replicas start serving sooner.

Agent execution layer: isolation without paying for idle time

The agent execution layer runs the code agents produce, and the projects here sit at different levels. Kata Containers and gVisor isolate a workload from the host kernel. agent-sandbox, from Kubernetes SIGs, manages sandboxed agents as Kubernetes resources, and Agent Substrate builds on it to pack many agents onto fewer workers. Hyperlight, a CNCF Sandbox project donated by Microsoft in 2024, works at a finer grain, inside the application itself.

Kata runs each pod in a lightweight VM with its own guest kernel, and the pod API stays the same. A workload opts in through its runtime class and nothing else about its deployment changes, which is why agent-sandbox can use Kata as a backend for sandboxed agents. Kata supports several virtual machine monitors, including Cloud Hypervisor, which Agent Substrate uses for its microVM class.

Agent Substrate addresses density by mapping a large set of stateful agents onto a smaller pool of pre-warmed workers, assigning work in real time, and suspending idle agents to object storage so they can be restored on demand. It isolates with gVisor by default, with an optional microVM class built on Kata and Cloud Hypervisor. Agents stay isolated, and you stop paying for them while they wait.

Hyperlight embeds a micro-VM manager in an application and runs guest code with no kernel or operating system inside the VM. VMs start in one to two milliseconds, and it can snapshot and restore VM memory.

Compute layer: bringing capacity to the cluster

The compute layer deals with fragmented GPU capacity. Karpenter and the Cluster Autoscaler add nodes as demand grows, and KubeFleet places work across clusters. Dynamic Resource Allocation (DRA), stable since Kubernetes 1.34, lets workloads request accelerators by their attributes rather than as an opaque device count.

Fragmented capacity can also be addressed from the other direction: bringing existing compute into a cluster’s scheduling domain. This allows workloads to use capacity across regions, on-premises environments, or edge locations through standard Kubernetes scheduling and policy. Open-source projects such as Flex nodes for AKS are exploring this model by connecting user-managed VMs and bare-metal hosts to an existing cluster as worker nodes.

The loop, end to end

Back to our CI agent example: when a build fails, Agent Substrate restores the agent from a snapshot onto a warm, sandboxed worker. The agent works the problem and is suspended again when it finishes, so it holds no compute between failures.

Its model calls go to an endpoint served from the model layer. Successful trajectories accumulate in storage, and on a schedule a Kueue-managed fine-tuning job lands on whatever GPU capacity is free, including nodes outside the cluster’s home region. The new checkpoint is evaluated and rolled out by updating the model’s desired state.

“With no second (or third) platform to stand up and no handoffs between them, the loop stays cheap enough to run repeatedly.”

Every stage runs on one control plane, under the same identity and policy, and shows up in the same observability tools. With no second (or third) platform to stand up and no handoffs between them, the loop stays cheap enough to run repeatedly.

Where to start

Open-weight models made it possible to own the model. The open-source ecosystem around them is what makes it practical to own the whole loop, from serving through retraining, without depending on a single provider for either. 

That said, much of this stack is still young. Agent Substrate, gVisor, KAITO, and Hyperlight are CNCF Sandbox projects, but Agent Substrate and Hyperlight remain pre-1.0. Their direction depends heavily on the people running them in production.

If you’re building a learning loop of your own, start with the layer where friction is highest today and run that project against your own workload – all these communities’ welcome issues, use cases, and contributions.

The post Postcards from tomorrow: Powering the agentic era through open source appeared first on The New Stack.
Open-weight models nearly match closed ones, so the model isn’t the bottleneck. The costly learning loop is, and Kubernetes can run all of it.

item.title: I broke a working agent seven ways. The metric I was watching caught two of them.
item.dc:creator: Kayode Ojo
item.description:
In September, I ran two models through the same 20 support tasks. Both scored 20 out of 20. Then I

The post I broke a working agent seven ways. The metric I was watching caught two of them. appeared first on The New Stack.
item.content:encoded:
In September, I ran two models through the same 20 support tasks. Both scored 20 out of 20. Then I assigned each model two refund requests that the underlying billing data didn’t support: one against an uncollected invoice, and one for double the invoice’s value.

Claude Haiku 4.5 issued all six refunds across three distinct permission configurations. Claude Sonnet 5 issued none. Their success rates looked identical, but their behavior diverged completely on the only scenarios capable of causing financial damage.

In October, I reran the evaluation harness. This time, the smaller model declined every unauthorized refund. I initially attributed this to queue ordering: the two trap tasks sat at the end of a 22-task queue instead of arriving in isolation, suggesting that processing 20 prior invoice tasks taught the agent to verify state before acting. I documented this theory in a neat report.

“Their success rates looked identical, but their behavior diverged completely on the only scenarios capable of causing financial damage.”

Then I checked the execution transcripts for the active model alias. In September, the haiku alias resolved to claude-haiku-4-5. In October, the same alias resolved to claude-haiku-5-5. I reran the isolated trap tasks three times against the new model version, and it declined all six attempts. Queue position had nothing to do with the outcome; the underlying model had been silently upgraded behind an unpinned alias. I discovered this only because of a script search I nearly skipped.

An unlogged, uninitiated deployment had occurred. Nothing in my high-level success metrics flagged the shift: 20 out of 20 in September, and 18 out of 19 on scored tasks in October (with the single failure stemming from an intentionally ambiguous prompt). Although the silent model update improved performance, the underlying monitoring gap remains concerning: none of the metrics I tracked would have alerted me if performance had degraded instead.

I stopped asking whether my agent was functioning and focused on a narrower diagnostic question: If I intentionally break the system, which metrics actually detect the failure?

Intentionally breaking the agent

The target system is a customer support agent interacting with a mock enterprise API spanning 30 scoped operations across tickets, users, billing, subscriptions, files, and messages. Every API call writes to an append-only audit log, and each task concludes with a state change that an external script verifies mechanically against the database. The suite contains 19 standard scored tasks alongside the two refund traps.

I established a baseline using Claude Sonnet 5.5 (claude-sonnet-5-5) with full administrative privileges across three identical runs. Evaluating three baseline replicates is critical: a detection system that fires false positives on an unmodified setup is useless. Every detection threshold reflects the baseline variance doubled to account for real-world statistical distribution.

I then introduced eight specific regressions—one per test run—to simulate common production failure modes:

  • Weaker model: Executed the standard prompt using Claude Haiku 5.5.
  • Speed pressure: Added a single instruction directing the agent to minimize API calls and skip optional read operations.
  • Truncated documentation: Restricted the API documentation to list only 11 of the 30 available commands.
  • Missing scope: Revoked one required permission per task from the credential grant.
  • Stale reads: Routed read queries to an asynchronous replica that lagged behind primary writes.
  • Flaky upstream API: Intercepted a deterministic 25% of API calls with transient errors.
  • Slow upstream API: Introduced 1.5 seconds of artificial latency to every network call.
  • Distractor tool: Exposed a deprecated alias alongside the valid close-ticket command that accepted calls without mutating state.

Six of these eight regressions execute inside the API behind a per-run wrapper script, ensuring deterministic, reproducible failure paths.

Before evaluating detector sensitivity, I verified that each injection actively affected the execution environment. A detector cannot catch an idle regression. The logs confirmed the flaky API arm intercepted 31 calls, the stale read arm served 18 outdated queries, and the missing-scope arm triggered 19 authorization denials.

The distractor arm invoked the deprecated alias zero times because the model selected the correct command on every attempt. I classified that regression as absorbed rather than missed, excluding it from detector denominators while retaining it as a false-positive control. As expected, an arm where no operational failure occurred triggered zero behavioral alerts.

Detection results

Detector thresholds derived from the baseline runs:

  • Task success: Fires below 18 of 19 verified completions.
  • Token cost: Fires outside a ±37% volume envelope.
  • Tool calls: Fires outside a ±7% call count envelope.
  • Scope drift: Fires above a 0.135 threshold (calculated as 1 – overlap between the active task scopes and baseline scopes, averaged across all tasks).

Across the seven active regressions, tool-call counts and scope drift each caught four failures. Task success rates caught only two. Token costs flagged one, while the refund trap tasks caught zero.

Task success rates flagged only the two regressions that made task completion physically impossible. Swapping the model, modifying system prompts, failing 25% of network calls, serving stale data from replicas, and adding 1.5 seconds of API latency all left task completion steady at 18 or 19 out of 19.

The speed-pressure arm requires context: the agent completed every task using 21% fewer calls and 17% fewer tokens. Two behavioral detectors flagged this run because the execution pattern shifted significantly, even though the shift improved efficiency. Behavioral detectors report movement; engineering teams must decide if that movement represents progress or degradation.

How competent agents mask infrastructure faults

AI agents routinely mask underlying technical failures through three primary behaviors:

1. Automated retry logic

The flaky API arm absorbed all 31 injected network failures. Before retrying non-idempotent write operations, the agent queried the backend to confirm if the initial attempt had committed, preventing duplicate refunds. One task—a subscription cancellation followed by a customer notification—absorbed seven consecutive API failures during execution.

“As agent retry logic improves, downstream task completion becomes increasingly decoupled from infrastructure health.”

The arm verified 19 out of 19 tasks while executing 99 tool calls against the 58-call baseline. As agent retry logic improves, downstream task completion becomes increasingly decoupled from infrastructure health.

2. Autonomous workarounds

When provided with documentation for only 11 of 30 commands, the agent recovered missing endpoints by guessing plausible command names. It batched hundreds of experimental attempts into shell loops, distinguishing valid endpoints from invalid ones based on returned error structures.

Through this brute-force approach, the agent successfully discovered refund, messaging, file upload, search, and admin endpoints. It failed to discover subscription commands, causing six tasks to fail.

This recovery process consumed 161,013 tokens (73% above baseline) and took 15 minutes to execute, compared to the five-minute baseline. Because the agent executed these speculative loops locally, the attempts never hit the API audit log. The regression remained detectable almost entirely due to its extreme token overhead.

3. Caution under uncertainty

The stale-read arm highlights the limits of quantitative monitoring. All write operations committed successfully to the primary database, but 18 subsequent read operations fetched outdated state from the lagging replica.

When the agent closed a ticket and re-read its status, the record appeared open. When it processed an invoice refund and re-read the balance, the refund appeared unapplied.

Token usage increased by 22% (below the 37% alert threshold), tool calls increased by 5% (below the 7% threshold), and scope drift reached 0.133 (below the 0.135 threshold). Every quantitative metric remained completely green.


Stale Read Execution Flow:
Write to Primary (Success) ──► Read from Replica (Stale Data Returned)
                                          │
                                          ▼
                        Agent Analyzes Discrepancy
                                          │
                                          ▼
                      Agent Suppresses Retries & Logs Warning

However, the agent’s final text summary explicitly detailed the anomaly. It reported that none of its 19 writes could be verified via read-backs, systematically laid out the evidence for each task, and explained that it deliberately suppressed retries for refunds, comments, messages, and uploads to avoid double-applying mutations.

“Its defensive caution successfully contained the fault, but simultaneously rendered a severe infrastructure issue invisible to quantitative monitoring.”

Had the agent blindly retried those operations, it would have generated duplicate refunds and triggered production alerts. Its defensive caution successfully contained the fault, but simultaneously rendered a severe infrastructure issue invisible to quantitative monitoring. The sole indicator of failure existed inside the prose summary.

Token usage is a noisy metric

Token consumption was the single metric already tracked across every run, yet it proved almost useless for anomaly detection. Baseline token usage fluctuated by 18% across three identical runs, forcing a wide ±37% detection threshold. Consequently, the +26% token surge from the flaky API arm and the +36% surge from the model swap both slipped beneath the alert line undetected.

By contrast, tool-call volume varied by only 3% across the same baseline runs, enabling a tight ±7% detection threshold that easily flagged the 70% surge in API calls. Teams alerting on execution costs should track tool-call volume rather than raw token counts.

The degradation of adversarial test sets

Adversarial test cases measure specific vulnerabilities in specific model generations. The refund traps successfully differentiated model capabilities in September, but caught zero errors in October because every tested arm—including standalone runs on the smaller model—declined the unauthorized actions.

Two variables shifted between test runs: the underlying model updated, and the launch prompt wording changed slightly. (The September transcripts needed to reconstruct the exact original prompt were cleared from temporary storage before analysis.) However, isolated reruns conclusively ruled out queue positioning as a factor.

Recommended monitoring stack for production agents

To effectively monitor autonomous agents, track these four telemetry layers:

  • Log the resolved model ID on every run: Treat any shift in the returned model string as an active production deployment.
  • Track tool calls per verified task against a replicated baseline: Measure call volume alongside task completion. In the flaky API test, tool calls surged 70% above the 58-call baseline despite a stable 19/19 completion rate, surfacing 31 hidden transient errors.
  • Isolate transient errors and retry attempts into explicit metrics: Track retries directly; they’re an early-warning indicator of infrastructure degradation that the agent is actively paying to mask.
  • Parse final agent summaries for explicit statements of uncertainty: Treat final agent reports as structured telemetry rather than plain text output. In the stale-read test, the summary contained the only indicator of system failure.
  • Rotate adversarial test sets whenever the underlying model updates: Existing test suites measure the limitations of previous model iterations. When a model updates, update the adversarial evaluations accordingly.

Validating your monitoring controls

To evaluate your telemetry layer, execute your agent’s unmodified baseline three times across identical tasks and calculate two variance metrics: tokens per task and tool calls per task. Expect the tool-call variance to be significantly tighter than the token variance (my test runs yielded 3% and 18%, respectively).

Next, inject transient failures into 25% of upstream network calls and execute the suite again. If your agent is appropriately resilient, overall task completion will remain stable while total tool calls roughly double. If task completion drops immediately, the agent’s retry logic requires improvement.

Running this benchmark reveals which telemetry layers can detect production degradation—providing the visibility needed to catch silent failures before an unannounced model swap forces an investigation.
