No Okta? No problem. Claude itself can now vouch for employees, so workplace plugins such as Notion, Figma, and Supabase connect automatically.

item.title: A developer opened Postman. Then two AI coding agents changed without their permission.
item.dc:creator: Amanda Caswell
item.description:
A developer says Postman’s desktop app installed plugins into Claude Code and OpenAI Codex without their permission. The app also

The post A developer opened Postman. Then two AI coding agents changed without their permission. appeared first on The New Stack.
item.content:encoded:
A developer says Postman’s desktop app installed plugins into Claude Code and OpenAI Codex without their permission. The app also tried to approve its own startup hook, which tells Codex to use Postman’s tools for API development tasks.

The developer, known as “indicava” on GitHub, reported the issue on October 25 after Codex began showing authentication errors and repeatedly loading Postman skills without being asked.

It’s raised concerns about how easily third-party applications can change how AI coding agents work, especially when those changes happen without a clear opt-in.

Plugins installed without permission

According to the report, opening Postman desktop version 12.33.4 on macOS triggered an installation process affecting both Claude Code and Codex.

Postman’s application logs, included in the GitHub issue, show an installation event on October 24 marked auto-existing-upgrade, with results indicating that plugins for both coding agents had been installed.

The developer also found changes to Codex’s user-level configuration file, ~/.codex/config.toml, including an enabled Postman plugin, a new plugin marketplace, and a trusted session-start hook.

The report also found a Postman CLI executable on the machine, with timestamps matching the installation.

Claude Code’s configuration similarly showed an installed Postman plugin. The report also found a Postman CLI executable on the machine, with timestamps matching the installation.

The developer says they had not explicitly authorized these changes. The report documents one macOS installation, and the behavior has not been independently reproduced across other systems.

The self-approving startup hook

But perhaps even more interesting is how Postman gets Codex to trust its plugin in the first place. According to Postman’s own documentation, its installer can automatically approve a session-start hook on the user’s behalf.

According to Postman’s own documentation, its installer can automatically approve a session-start hook on the user’s behalf.

Developers who install the plugin directly through Codex, however, must review and approve the hook themselves. The installer’s source code shows exactly what happens.

Postman checks whether Codex already trusts the hook. If it doesn’t, the installer uses config/batchWrite to add the hook’s trusted hash to Codex’s configuration. It checks that the hook hasn’t changed before approving it, and if approval fails or can’t be confirmed, it logs a message telling the developer to review the hook in Codex.

Session-start hooks can give coding agents instructions automatically, even when the developer hasn’t asked for them. Postman’s startup instructions tell Codex to load the postman:api-engineer skill before handling most API development tasks.

Codex is still supposed to follow the developer’s instructions first. But for many API tasks, it’s also being told to use Postman’s tools by default, whether the developer asked for them or not.

That might be useful for developers who chose to install the plugin. The concern here is that Postman’s desktop app reportedly added those instructions to an existing coding environment without the developer’s permission.

Developers raise security concerns

The findings have drawn criticism from developers on GitHub and X. Security researcher Frank Denis called the integrations “junk” on X and pointed out that Postman’s installer attempts to trust its own startup hook.

Siddharth Garimella went further, claiming that Postman’s hooks intercept API data and send it back to the company. However, the GitHub report provides no evidence that Postman collected or transmitted API data. It documents changes to agent settings and a remote MCP connection, not data theft.

The developer also found that Postman had configured a connection to its remote MCP server at https://mcp.postman.com/mcp, but Codex repeatedly failed to authenticate.

The criticism has also spread to GitHub, where one commenter calls the behavior “unacceptable, even creating risk in corporate environment.” Another urges Postman to be transparent and ask for permission.

Who controls the agent

The developer wants Postman to stop installing plugins for existing users without their permission and leave hook approval up to Codex. They also want a way to fully undo the changes.

Postman provides an uninstall command, but the developer says that isn’t enough. Removing the integration should also clear any changes to agent settings, trusted hooks, MCP connections, and installed CLI tools.

For now, developers can check their Claude Code and Codex settings for unfamiliar plugins, hooks, or MCP connections.

Postman’s installer can approve its own Codex hook without the usual manual review.

The complaint comes as developers are pushing for more control over their coding agents. Postman’s installer can approve its own Codex hook without the usual manual review. What remains unanswered is why an existing desktop installation reportedly triggered that process without the user’s permission.

The New Stack reached out to Postman to ask about the automatic installations, hook approvals, and user consent. The company had not responded by the time of publication.

The post A developer opened Postman. Then two AI coding agents changed without their permission. appeared first on The New Stack.
A developer found Postman’s desktop app installed plugins into Claude Code and Codex without permission, reviving questions about coding agent control.

item.title: Can agent standards keep up with the companies building them?
item.dc:creator: Frederic Lardinois
item.description:
Mazin Gilbert, executive director of the Linux Foundation’s Agentic AI Foundation, left Google earlier this year to lead the new AAIF,

The post Can agent standards keep up with the companies building them? appeared first on The New Stack.
item.content:encoded:
Mazin Gilbert, executive director of the Linux Foundation’s Agentic AI Foundation, left Google earlier this year to lead the new AAIF, and he recently shared with The New Stack a truth central to its mission: The AAIF has to move faster than its members.

Gilbert, speaking in an interview at AGNTCon + MCPCon North America in San Jose last month, said on The New Stack podcast, “If this foundation does not move at the speed of light, it becomes irrelevant.”

He also talked about how he gets OpenAI, Anthropic, and Google to agree on standards — even though they compete on products. Those companies are going to build products “with and without the standards,” he says.

All of this is happening while the foundation’s own members are often still figuring out how to build and use agents themselves. Some contribute to protocols and ship products, but others are still trying to get their agents out of the lab and into production. Gilbert says a third group of companies “frankly are panicking,” because they don’t have an agent strategy yet.

The San Jose event drew 4,300 registrants, he says, double the size of the foundation’s previous largest event in Amsterdam earlier this year.

How MCP gets built

Before our recording, Gilbert had just met with a group of maintainers from “very fiercely competing companies” who were working on the protocols together. All of those companies depend on these standards, he says, so they have a reason to get the work done.

“These protocols are the air you breathe.”
—Mazin Gilbert, executive director, AAIF.

“These protocols are the air you breathe. These protocols are the plumbing,” Gilbert says. “They may not be that sexy, maybe, but if we don’t get those right, that entire agentic AI space will be a mess, expensive and prohibitive basically for any company to deploy this at scale.”

As an example, he points to the July release of the Model Context Protocol (MCP) specification, which made the protocol stateless. “Every one of those companies not only contributed to it, but they ended up completely updating their entire stack to the stateless MCP,” he says.

MCP downloads grew tenfold in the protocol’s first 10 months at the foundation, according to Gilbert, after Anthropic donated it last December. Today, fewer than 15 percent of its maintainers work at Anthropic, and more than 1,000 organizations contribute 75 percent of the pull requests, he says. Those contributors include U.S. retailers and companies around the world.

At the Cloud Native Computing Foundation (CNCF), many projects started at startups before they were donated. At the AAIF, Gilbert says, large companies tend to contribute the protocols, and smaller companies extend them and build businesses on top.

Some of those startups were doing something “very different” six months or a year ago, he says, and some didn’t exist yet. Now they’re building enterprise products on MCP and the foundation’s gateway projects to connect agents to companies’ back-end systems.

Getting members to contribute

The AAIF now has 305 members, and Gilbert said in his keynote that about one new company joins every business day. He calls it the fastest-growing foundation in the Linux Foundation’s history. About 40 percent of its members are startups, and 19 percent are nonprofits, national labs, and academic institutions.

“None of us have done this before, so I just want to be very clear about that. We are learning this as we go,” he says.

Part of the job is making membership worth enough that companies actively contribute. “It’s not about the money. Their time is far more valuable than their money. Their people are far more valuable than the money,” Gilbert says.

He’d like every member to contribute, but also acknowledges that’s not the case yet. He knows who does, because he uses his own agents to track contributions across the foundation.

Some companies are still trying to understand what agents can do for them and what they’d get back on the investment. Others don’t know how to contribute. Gilbert encourages them to start by joining a working group and listening, and says they don’t have to arrive as experts. For companies still learning, the foundation launched its first certification in September: the Model Context Protocol Associate (MCPA).

The Gates Foundation, which joined in September, now sits on the AAIF’s board. Gilbert says it’s helping developers in parts of Africa and South Asia get the training and certification they need to contribute, and to attend events they couldn’t otherwise afford.

Pressed on whether nonprofits and for-profit companies clash inside the foundation, Gilbert says he hasn’t seen it yet. “Whether you are a nonprofit, for-profit, small, large, your value, your impact, your power in this foundation really depends on contributions,” he says.

How many gateways do you need?

The foundation is also choosing which projects to accept. The community has submitted 65 projects through its public intake process, Gilbert says, and the AAIF has declined some. The first 10 to 20 projects “really define the DNA of this foundation,” he says.

With the four projects it announced in San Jose (Agent Skills from Anthropic, Open Responses from OpenAI, OpenEnv from Hugging Face, and OpenSandbox from Alibaba), the AAIF now hosts 10.

In some cases, the foundation is taking in technologies that are already widely adopted, like MCP and Agent Skills. In others, nobody agrees yet on what a standard should look like.

Gateways are one example. The AAIF approved two gateway projects this year, Solo.io’s agentgateway and Agent Router, which moved over from the CNCF’s Envoy project in September. Gilbert says five or six more companies want to contribute their own. Does the community need “six gateways or 10 gateways,” he asks, “or do we need to harmonize those together?”

He doesn’t have an answer yet, and says the community doesn’t either. The foundation gives those companies neutral governance to work it out together, he says.

The technical committee and governing board evaluate each proposal, including whether the AAIF is the right home for it, Gilbert says. They look at every layer of the stack, including agent frameworks, execution harnesses, gateways, guardrails, memory, protocols, observability, and identity. Not every project the foundation accepts will become the standard, he notes.

Agents that can transact

Gilbert wants the foundation to work on identity, security, trust, and observability. He also wants it to take on agent commerce.

“These agents, the internet of agents, must be transactional,” he says. An agent making a purchase would need to discover a catalog, talk to a merchant’s agent, negotiate, pay, and handle returns or disputes, and Gilbert says each step still needs a protocol.

He’s also excited about physical AI, meaning protocols for agents that talk to machines and appliances instead of databases. “Your refrigerator, your washing machines. It’s so cool,” he says. “It’s like science fiction, but it’s happening now.”

Wherever the protocols fall short, Gilbert says, companies will write custom code, and customers will end up paying to support it. A standard that arrives after a customer has built and deployed its own integration still leaves that customer with code to maintain.

The post Can agent standards keep up with the companies building them? appeared first on The New Stack.

item.title: Goldman Sachs restricted Claude Code for bankers — but made one surprising exception
item.dc:creator: Amanda Caswell
item.description:
Replit CEO Amjad Masad is warning that AI coding agents running on employee devices are becoming a security risk for

The post Goldman Sachs restricted Claude Code for bankers — but made one surprising exception appeared first on The New Stack.
item.content:encoded:
Replit CEO Amjad Masad is warning that AI coding agents running on employee devices are becoming a security risk for enterprises and governments, as financial institutions begin restricting access to tools such as Claude Code.

“AI agents running on employee endpoints are becoming a systemic security risk for enterprises & governments,” Masad writes on X, Tuesday. “Some are responding by restricting tools like Claude Code, as Goldman Sachs reportedly has.”

“Some are responding by restricting tools like Claude Code, as Goldman Sachs reportedly has.”

Why finance restricts coding agents

His comments follow a Bloomberg report that Goldman Sachs has restricted access to Anthropic’s Claude Code and Microsoft’s GitHub coding tools to engineers. The restrictions apply to bankers and traders, but certain quantitative employees known as strats are exempt.

Goldman spokesperson Nick Carcaterra told Bloomberg the bank weighs productivity gains against potential risks when deciding which employees can continue using AI tools.

Masad suggests Goldman Sachs is not alone.

“This is widespread in finance. The ban hammer is coming down,”

“This is widespread in finance. The ban hammer is coming down,” he writes, responding to a post about the bank’s restrictions.

When asked what was driving the crackdown, Masad points to “Supply chain attacks etc.”

The credential exposure problem

Running coding agents directly on employee machines raises concerns about credential exposure, malicious instructions and compromised dependencies, each of which has already surfaced well beyond the finance sector.

The credential question has been pushing vendors toward short-lived tokens for months, a shift Vercel recently forced on its own suppliers by setting a deadline to abandon the long-lived keys that an agent operating on an endpoint could quietly read and reuse.

When asked on X whether banks were more worried about code leaving their environments or a lack of audit trails, Masad says, “So many things.”

He offered no examples of security incidents that prompted Goldman’s restrictions or other financial institutions adopting similar policies.

Isolating agents in the cloud

Alongside his comments, Masad shares a security advisory published by Replit on Monday. Written by Luis Héctor Chávez, Replit’s chief technology officer, and engineering lead at Replit, Manish Mehta, it recommends keeping AI agents off employee devices and running them in company-controlled cloud environments instead.

“AI agents should operate in dedicated, organization-controlled environments with limited access to the resources each task requires,”

“AI agents should operate in dedicated, organization-controlled environments with limited access to the resources each task requires,” Masad writes.

Replit recommends running agents in isolated environments, with credentials, audit logs, and approvals managed separately.

The advisory points to recent security incidents, including a compromised Claude Code extension distributed through the Cursor marketplace, as an example of how attackers can exploit developer tools.

That pattern has played out repeatedly across the ecosystem this year, including an attack in which intruders hijacked roughly 1,900 GitHub accounts before moving against some 30,000 repositories, a reminder that a single poisoned link in the chain can reach far past the machine where it started.

Controlling what agents can access

But restricting AI coding agents to engineers doesn’t necessarily solve the problem. Even experienced developers can run agents that follow malicious instructions or pull in compromised software, and research has shown how little it takes to knock an agent off course, with one team finding that stripping a single line from Claude Code’s instructions sent its out-of-scope actions climbing. Replit argues that companies need to control what agents can do, not just who gets to use them.

What this means for enterprise AI adoption

Goldman’s restrictions suggest companies may be rethinking how widely they allow employees to use AI coding tools. Giving non-developers the ability to build software has been a major selling point, but that becomes harder to justify when agents have access to sensitive corporate systems.

Masad argues that companies don’t need to stop using agents. They need to keep them off employee devices and put tighter controls around what they can access.

Whether financial institutions broadly adopt that model remains to be seen. Masad has described restrictions as widespread, but has not provided public evidence establishing how many organizations have introduced them.

The New Stack has reached out to Replit for additional comment on the reported restrictions, the security concerns driving them, and whether financial institutions are changing their approach to AI coding agents.

The post Goldman Sachs restricted Claude Code for bankers — but made one surprising exception appeared first on The New Stack.
Replit’s CEO says AI coding agents on employee devices are a growing security risk, as banks like Goldman Sachs restrict tools such as Claude Code.

item.title: Anthropic speeds up Claude Code with message threads. But your token bill stays the same.
item.dc:creator: Paul Sawers
item.description:
Anthropic has announced a new feature that aims to speed up long-running Claude Code sessions by reducing the amount of

The post Anthropic speeds up Claude Code with message threads. But your token bill stays the same. appeared first on The New Stack.
item.content:encoded:
Anthropic has announced a new feature that aims to speed up long-running Claude Code sessions by reducing the amount of conversation data repeatedly sent to its API, helping developers get responses faster as their coding sessions grow.

Message threads, as it’s called, is available now in public beta for Anthropic’s Messages API and is already enabled by default for “most” Claude Code users, according to an article published by Anthropic on Monday.

The company says that the feature has reduced median time to first token (TTFT) — the time it takes Claude to begin generating a response — by approximately 35% for Claude Code requests containing between 500,000 and 1 million tokens.

Given that it’s now part of the Messages API, the feature also extends beyond Claude Code to developers building their own AI agents, particularly those handling lengthy conversations, repeated tool calls, and large amounts of data.

How message threads works

To understand what’s changed, it’s worth looking at how the Messages API has traditionally handled conversations.

Every time an agent sends a new request to Claude, it includes the entire conversation history. That means all messages and tool calls must be transmitted again, even though the API has previously received them.

For example, a coding agent working through a complex task will likely entail hundreds of API calls. As it reads files and modifies code, the conversation history grows, and by the time that history reaches 500,000 tokens, every subsequent request requires sending those 500,000 tokens again, along with whatever new information has been thrown into the mix.

The API then has to validate and tokenize the incoming data before Claude can begin responding. This rinse-and-repeat processing can add significant latency, particularly during lengthy coding sessions.

And so message threads switches things up by allowing Anthropic to temporarily retain the conversation history on its servers. The first request still sends the complete conversation, including any system prompts and tool definitions. But subsequent requests need only contain new messages and a reference to the previous response.

Behind the scenes, Anthropic reconstructs the full conversation on its servers before passing it to Claude, negating the need for the client to keep uploading the same information. This detail is important, because Claude still processes the entire conversation on every turn — if the history contains 500,000 tokens, the model still receives that context, even though the client has transmitted only the latest messages.

“While each request is smaller with message threads, Claude still reads the full conversation on every turn, so token usage stays the same.”

As such, message threads doesn’t inherently reduce API costs — Anthropic continues to charge for the tokens Claude processes. “While each request is smaller with message threads, Claude still reads the full conversation on every turn, so token usage stays the same,” the company notes.

Developers can, however, combine message threads with Claude’s existing prompt caching feature, which allows previously processed content to be reused at discounted token rates. The two features can work in tandem to reduce latency and processing costs respectively.

Anthropic identifies several use-cases where message threads could be particularly useful. These include long-running coding agents that accumulate file edits and tool results, computer-use agents that repeatedly capture screenshots, and applications handling large volumes of documents or images. In each case, avoiding repeated uploads reduces the amount of data transmitted during a session.

Guillaume Lebedel, co-founder and CTO of AI agent infrastructure company StackOne, took to LinkedIn on Tuesday to illustrate the potential benefits of message threads for computer-use agents, using a simulation to estimate how much data could be saved.

His calculations assume an agent captures one 150 KB screenshot at each step. Without message threads, the 50th request would need to upload approximately 7.5 MB of accumulated screenshots. With message threads, that request would carry just the latest screenshot, approximately 0.15 MB.

Across the entire 50-step session, the cumulative screenshot data uploaded would fall from roughly 191 MB to 7.5 MB — a reduction of approximately 25 times.

While these figures aren’t based on a live API test, they illustrate the potential benefits for agents that repeatedly upload large files. Indeed, Lebedel predicts that computer-use agents could spearhead adoption of the feature, with widespread uptake before the end of the year.

“My bet — computer-use agents adopt it before coding agents do, since a screenshot per step is what makes the resend heavy.”

“My bet — computer-use agents adopt it before coding agents do, since a screenshot per step is what makes the resend heavy, and most have it on by the end of December,” he writes.

How to use message threads

To implement the feature, Anthropic has introduced a new thread parameter to the Messages API. The initial request creates a thread by including thread={"type": "create"}, alongside the full conversation history, system prompt, and any tools being used.

Subsequent requests use thread={"type": "continue", "previous_message_id": first.id}, where first.id refers to the response ID returned by the initial request.

These follow-up requests contain only the new messages. The API retains the earlier conversation and its original system prompt and tool definitions.

Because the feature remains in beta, developers making requests directly must also include the anthropic-beta header with the value message-threads-2026-08-12. In the Python SDK, this can be supplied through betas=["message-threads-2026-08-12"].

Anthropic also provides a simpler approach through its SDK thread helper, which manages the conversation history and API parameters automatically.

Using the Python SDK, developers first create a client with client = anthropic.Anthropic(), before initialising a thread through client.beta.messages.thread(). The latter accepts the model, maximum output tokens and initial system prompt, among other parameters.

Once configured, developers use thread.send() to submit messages. The SDK thread helper automatically creates the thread on the first request, then continues it on subsequent turns, supplying the necessary parameters and retaining a local copy of the conversation history.

The SDK thread helper also adds the required beta header automatically, removing the need for developers to specify it with each request.

Message threads expire

There is, however, one notable limitation in all of this. Message threads expire after just five minutes of inactivity. And as one user observed on X, “Five minutes at the coffee machine and the thread expires.”

Another user went further, writing: “Only 5 minutes for cache expires is almost useless.” The user appears to be referring to the message thread expiry, which is separate from Claude’s prompt caching feature.

“Five minutes at the coffee machine and the thread expires.”

That might seem like an unforgiving restriction for a feature designed to improve lengthy coding sessions, however the implications are perhaps not so dramatic. If a developer steps away for ten minutes, say, the thread will indeed have expired. However, provided the client has retained the conversation history, the SDK helper automatically resends it to establish a new thread when they return. So the first request after a break may therefore take longer, but the coding session can continue without losing its previous context.

For agents operating continuously, the limitation may be even less consequential. Every successful request stored in the thread refreshes the five-minute expiry period, meaning an agent making regular API calls can maintain the same thread throughout a lengthy task.

Developers managing threads directly must handle expiry themselves. An attempt to continue an unavailable thread returns a 404 error, requiring the client to resend the complete conversation and establish a new thread.

There are also some data-handling considerations. Anthropic says thread contents are encrypted and held in server memory without being written to persistent storage. Although threads expire after five minutes of inactivity, their contents may remain in memory for up to an hour after their last use.

The feature is currently ineligible for zero data retention and HIPAA, which could restrict its use in environments with stringent data-handling requirements. Certain context-management capabilities, including on-demand compaction, are also unsupported.

Message threads is available across all Claude models in beta, including through Claude Platform on AWS, Claude in Microsoft Foundry, and Anthropic-managed Claude Models on Google Cloud.

The post Anthropic speeds up Claude Code with message threads. But your token bill stays the same. appeared first on The New Stack.
Message threads stop Claude Code resending whole conversations. They expire after five minutes idle, though, so maybe don’t take that coffee break.

item.title: OpenAI built itself a new Git backend, too
item.dc:creator: Frederic Lardinois
item.description:
OpenAI on Monday detailed how it built a new Git backend for its monorepo to power the ever-increasing number of

The post OpenAI built itself a new Git backend, too appeared first on The New Stack.
item.content:encoded:
OpenAI on Monday detailed how it built a new Git backend for its monorepo to power the ever-increasing number of commits its developers and their agents now create.

Pando, as the team calls the new backend, cut push latency by nearly 5x, the company says, and it currently serves close to a petabyte of Git data per day at OpenAI.

OpenAI is obviously an early adopter of agentic coding tools. Compared to the first quarter of 2024, the quarterly commits to its monorepo will have increased by over 2,400% by the end of this year, the company says. But the issues it is facing are similar to what many other enterprises and Git forges like GitHub are now seeing.

With the pace of development increasing, Git itself is becoming a bottleneck. GitHub, for example, spent much of its recent Universe keynote on how it is improving its infrastructure to become faster and more reliable, all while serving billions of pull requests every month.

That has given rise to startups like Entire (from former GitHub CEO Thomas Dohmke) and projects like Origin from Cursor. Like OpenAI’s work, those are based on Git, but others, like Anthropic, basically start from scratch with a new client and architecture.

Why OpenAI stayed with Git

The OpenAI team explicitly notes that it wanted to retain compatibility with Git. The team was seeing the reliability of its Git backend fall below 90%, with slow fetches and failed merges, but decided to stay within the Git ecosystem.

As OpenAI’s Aaron Friel, Taylor Blau, and Ted Nyman ask in the announcement, the question the team asked itself was if it had “reached a limit of Git itself, or of the way we served our monorepo?” The answer for OpenAI was that the Git client and protocol weren’t really the problem (though the team is also making some tweaks there), but the way conventional Git servers are built.

“For more than two decades, developers have adapted their tools around Git as the way they build software has changed,” they write. “When we started to feel friction in our own monorepo, it mattered to us that we could keep building on that work.”

How Pando works

Pando drops two things most Git servers treat as requirements. The first is keeping every branch in the repository in a consistent state at once. The second is building a custom packfile, Git’s format for bundling compressed objects, for every client that fetches code.

In Git, a branch is simply a pointer to that latest commit. Moving that pointer is the only part of a push that requires coordination. Conventional Git servers order those updates across the entire repository, so when there are many developers working in parallel, a push to one agent’s branch can end up waiting on another’s.

Pando, on the other hands, doesn’t coordinate every write across the whole repository. Instead, it handles each branch on its own. Because of this, pushes to unrelated branches then don’t have to wait on each other.

There’s a tradeoff here, the team acknowledges. When a client is looking at several branches at once, it may see them at slightly different points in time. In practice, however, users and agents only care about the order of updates to a single branch, OpenAI argues.

When a client pushes, Pando validates the incoming packfile as it streams it into blob storage, without unpacking it into a local repository. It records the new branch tip, the packfile’s location, and its dependencies in a metadata store. By default, Pando advertises only the trunk branch as a base for feature-branch pushes. That makes each pack reusable by other clients that already have the advertised trunk history.

Then, when another client fetches the branch, Pando selects the stored packs it needs based on the history it already has. It then returns download links through packfile-uri, a Git protocol feature that lets clients download packs separately.

A caching service called Express then serves those packs from regional caches, with a hit rate above 99%, the company says. On standard cloud VMs, clones and fetches can max out a 10 Gbps network link.

A busy monorepo would otherwise leave clients downloading tens of thousands of small packs a day, so background workers merge them into larger ones over time, much like a log-structured database compacts its data. That also lets Pando work out which packs a client needs in logarithmic time.

Pando vs. standard Git servers

On a standard Git server, every fetch means working out which objects the client is missing and compressing a fresh packfile just for that client. Those packs are expensive to generate and hard to cache, OpenAI says. Pando mostly hands out bytes it already has.

Before a push, a regular Git server also lists every branch it holds so the client can skip objects the server already has. With millions of branches, that list alone can grow past 100 MiB, according to OpenAI. Advertising only trunk keeps it small, but it means repeat pushes to the same branch resend everything that isn’t on trunk. The team says that’s a fair trade, since the median pack in its monorepo is still under 20 KiB.

Regular Git servers also have to repack and garbage-collect repositories to keep them fast, which eats up compute and disk I/O. Pando never throws a pack away. It keeps packs at every compaction level and serves from all of them.

For developers, little of this is visible. They keep using standard Git commands, though OpenAI now ships its own Git build to developer machines and inside the ChatGPT desktop app.

OpenAI built Pando in Rust in 10 weeks, with one engineer designing the core and teams of Codex agents implementing it. It went into production in April.

What goes back into open source Git?

Building on Git also meant running into some of Git’s own rough edges, and OpenAI says it’s sending many of its fixes back to the project. Because Pando leans so heavily on packfile-uri, which a Google engineer first proposed in 2019, the team had to fix how the Git client handles concurrent pack downloads, cleans up after interrupted transfers, and resumes downloads that had already finished. It also added tracing for those downloads, which makes it easier to tell whether a slow fetch is spending its time generating packs or transferring them.

Not all of that work has landed in Git yet. OpenAI says several of its changes are already upstream, while many others for now only live in the company’s public Git repository. Those include support for downloading and indexing packs in parallel and a new “explicit haves” feature, which lets a server tell a pushing client where a branch currently points without letting the client leave that history out of its pack. The company is tracking all of this in a public patch tracker.

Pando itself isn’t part of that, though. OpenAI isn’t open sourcing the backend, and as of now, it only says that it’s looking into ways to share the underlying technology with its users. Anthropic, too, has said it has no plans to release Scion, either.

The post OpenAI built itself a new Git backend, too appeared first on The New Stack.
Unlike Anthropic, OpenAI kept Git. Its new backend, Pando, cut push latency nearly 5x and serves close to a petabyte of Git data a day.

item.title: Developers are downgrading their AI on purpose — and it’s working
item.dc:creator: Amanda Caswell
item.description:
Anthropic has confirmed that it added new restrictions to Claude Code to prevent users from recreating existing video games. But

The post Developers are downgrading their AI on purpose — and it’s working appeared first on The New Stack.
item.content:encoded:
Anthropic has confirmed that it added new restrictions to Claude Code to prevent users from recreating existing video games. But developers say Claude Opus 5.5 is also refusing reverse-engineering and software-analysis tasks it previously handled, raising questions about what else Anthropic may have changed.

For some developers, the refusals are already affecting their work. One developer says paid client projects have stalled because Claude Code won’t work on existing games, while others say the model is refusing to analyze software. At least one developer got back to work by switching to an older Claude model.

On Friday, Addy Osmani, a member of Anthropic’s technical team, confirmed on X that the company had deliberately modified Claude Code’s instructions.

“We added two sentences to Claude Code’s prompt on Opus 5.5 to steer it away from recreating someone else’s specific game because using Claude to infringe IP is against our usage policy.”

“We added two sentences to Claude Code’s prompt on Opus 5.5 to steer it away from recreating someone else’s specific game because using Claude to infringe IP is against our usage policy,” Osmani writes.

He clarifies that developers should still be able to create original games, build within established genres and work with their own designs and assets.

“We’ll continue to iterate to ensure we’re striking the right balance,” he adds, inviting developers to contact him if Claude refuses work involving their own creations.

Anthropic has not publicly confirmed whether the reverse engineering refusals are tied to the new instructions or to separate cybersecurity restrictions.

Reverse engineering hits a wall

The complaints extend beyond game development. Developers say Opus 5.5 is refusing software-analysis tasks that previously worked. Technical writer for Phison Electronics USA, Jarred Walton encountered refusals while testing software he was developing, but switching to Opus 4.8 allowed him to continue.

While Anthropic is trying to prevent misuse without blocking legitimate development work, developers are left unable to do tasks as Claude Code suddenly refuses what it once handled, with little explanation for the change.

developers are left unable to do tasks as Claude Code suddenly refuses what it once handled, with little explanation for the change.

Paid client work stalls out

On October 30, Ray Weiss, founder and CEO of Conflict Simulations LLC, reported on GitHub that Claude Code had stopped working on paid client projects it had supported for months.

His company creates custom digital versions of board wargames for clients who own the physical games. Weiss says the projects use original code and client-supplied materials, but Claude Code now refuses to continue the work because of its restrictions on recreating existing games.

Weiss wants Anthropic to distinguish between infringement and commissioned development, offer a verification process, and document major changes to Claude Code’s instructions.

The hosted agent risk

The complaint highlights a larger problem with hosted coding agents. Anthropic can change what Claude Code will or won’t do without developers changing their code, tools, or prompts. Work that was possible one day may suddenly be blocked the next.

Work that was possible one day may suddenly be blocked the next.

On October 6, Anthropic expanded its Cyber Verification Program, giving vetted security researchers access to fewer restrictions after acknowledging that its safeguards can block legitimate cybersecurity work.

It’s still unclear whether those safeguards are behind the latest refusals, especially since developers say they can complete some of the same tasks using older Claude models.

Developers are left guessing

Reverse engineering has legitimate uses well beyond security research. In October, Red Hat engineering director Christian Schaller used Claude Code to help reverse engineer a scanner driver, bringing Linux support to hardware whose manufacturer had changed its chipset.

Anthropic has acknowledged that its game-cloning restrictions need refinement, but developers still don’t know why Claude Code is refusing some reverse-engineering tasks that previously worked, or which workflows could be affected next.

The New Stack reached out to Anthropic regarding whether the refusals are tied to its new game-cloning restrictions or other safeguards. The company did not respond before publication.

The post Developers are downgrading their AI on purpose — and it’s working appeared first on The New Stack.
Anthropic added game-cloning limits to Claude Code, but developers say Opus 5.5 is now refusing reverse-engineering and software work it once handled.

item.title: Your AI coding agent now runs on a budget — and it can cut you off mid-task
item.dc:creator: Amanda Caswell
item.description:
The days of pointing an AI agent at a backlog and letting it burn through compute without much oversight may

The post Your AI coding agent now runs on a budget — and it can cut you off mid-task appeared first on The New Stack.
item.content:encoded:
The days of pointing an AI agent at a backlog and letting it burn through compute without much oversight may be coming to an end. Cognition is introducing hierarchical budgets for Devin so enterprises can manage AI coding agent spending across departments, projects, and individual engineers. Administrators can assign budgets to different teams, track how much each one spends, and approve more capacity based on engineering efficiency. There’s a catch for developers, though; if a budget runs out while Devin is working on a task, the session stops.

If a budget runs out while Devin is working on a task, the session stops.

The feature grew out of conversations with customers, according to Lukas Burger, who works across go-to-market and engineering at Cognition. “Most of what we build starts with our forward deployed engineers (FDEs), who work on-site with customers. Budgets came straight out of those conversations,” Burger tells The New Stack. Once Devin moved past pilots and into broader deployments across organizations, he explains, the blunt controls that had worked for a single team — org limits, per-user tiers, and separate Devin Desktop settings — stopped holding up.

From Pilots to the P&L

The problem Budgets sets out to solve is one of scale and sprawl rather than raw price. “That’s fine for one team. It doesn’t hold up when a bank is dividing a large ACU commitment across hundreds of groups,” Burger tells The New Stack of the older spending controls. Some of those customers had started building and maintaining their own internal tools just to parcel out capacity to the leaders of each business line, a workaround that mapped the exact gap Cognition set out to close.

Cognition built the feature with some of the world’s largest enterprises as design partners, testing the model with customers managing millions of Agent Compute Units, the consumption-based units used to measure the work Devin performs.

Burger is keeping quiet on individual customer spending figures, but he is clear about what changes as deployments widen. “Devin stops belonging to one team,” he says. “A pilot might sit with a single platform group. A broad rollout means many departments, each with its own priorities and its own budget owner.”

Budgets follow the org chart

Budgets is designed to work with the way enterprises already manage spending, meaning, an administrator starts with one overall budget, divides it among business units, and from there, those leaders can distribute funds to their own teams and projects, with budgets extending up to three levels deep. Central IT can still see where the money is going and set limits without approving every request. “The enterprise keeps guardrails and visibility across all of it,” Burger says.

Companies can also set aside budgets for specific projects rather than tying all spending to individual teams. A major legacy modernization effort, for example, could have its own budget even if engineers from several departments are working on it. Separate controls apply to Devin running in the cloud and on engineers’ desktops, so companies can track and limit spending in both environments.

When a budget runs out

The promise is that none of this should intrude on the work. “We designed Budgets so engineers can do their work without thinking about them,” Burger says, and the mechanics warn engineers before spending limits interrupt their sessions.

Engineers see alerts on their homepage when they are on track to exceed a limit, and they can request more ACUs from the budget owner without leaving the product. Each budget’s administrators decide whether to review those requests manually or clear them automatically.

Grading engineers on efficiency

That automation is where the feature turns pointed. Admins can enable efficiency-based approvals, which automatically lift an engineer’s limit when their Efficiency Score is strong, up to a ceiling the admin sets. Cognition introduced the scoring system in October to estimate productive engineering hours relative to Devin consumption, which permits administrators to allocate more capacity to engineers who appear to get more useful work from their usage. The score estimates efficiency, however, and does not directly measure code quality or business outcomes.

When a budget does empty, the session stops, which is why Burger frames the alerts and in-product requests as the first line of defense rather than the last.

“We’re also working on letting teams switch to lower-cost models after a soft limit, so important work can finish,”

“We’re also working on letting teams switch to lower-cost models after a soft limit, so important work can finish,” Burger tells The New Stack. That option is still in development, so for now, budget increases and advance warnings are the most effective ways to avoid interruptions to date.

Cognition is just as wary of the opposite failure, the controls drawn so tight they strangle the productivity they were meant to protect. “We also don’t want controls so tight that customers stop being productive with Devin,” Burger tells The New Stack, which is why the company suggests defaults with enough headroom to keep productive users from being blocked unnecessarily.

Much of the surprise in agent spending, he notes, “comes from not knowing where usage lands,” a gap that cheaper tokens alone may not close when agents run complex, multi-step tasks and a round of price cuts doesn’t necessarily translate into a smaller bill.

Proof in the Pull Requests

Consumption pricing cuts both ways, and Cognition knows it. “With consumption pricing, customers who can’t see value stop using the product, so we’ve put a lot of work into cost control and measurement,” Burger tells The New Stack.

“With consumption pricing, customers who can’t see value stop using the product, so we’ve put a lot of work into cost control and measurement,”

Each Devin session is tied to a specific budget, so companies can see exactly how much individual teams, projects or business units are spending. Instead of looking at one company-wide total, leaders can track the cost of a particular initiative. Some customers also link that spending to internal billing codes or charge it back to individual departments.

Measuring consumption is the easy half of the equation. For the harder question of whether the money is well spent, Burger says most customers fall back on the metrics they already trust, tracking merged pull requests, productive engineering hours, and DORA metrics.

Burger says the teams getting the most out of Devin look at business results, citing “how much faster the roadmap moves, how much unplanned work goes away, and how much less they spend on engineering toil.”

FinOps for AI agents

Burger doesn’t hesitate when asked whether agent budgeting is becoming a discipline of its own, much like FinOps did for cloud infrastructure. “Yes, and it’s already starting,” he tells The New Stack. Because agents are billed by consumption, finance teams are asking familiar questions about who is spending, where the money is going and whether it’s worth it. Burger says the shift is happening faster than it did with cloud computing because companies already have processes in place to manage those costs.

The FinOps Foundation’s 2026 “State of FinOps” report quantifies how far that has spread, finding that 98% of its 1,192 survey respondents now manage AI spending, up from 31% two years ago. Companies are still working out how to connect that spending with measurable returns. What makes Cognition’s approach different is that companies can manage budgets, assign spending limits and track costs directly in Devin instead of relying on separate tools.

Burger expects the responsibility to land squarely on finance teams. “I see this becoming a major new responsibility for strategic finance and FP&A teams,” he tells The New Stack. “On top of their day jobs, they’re now managing massive AI budgets and making sure that spend shows up as real impact on the P&L.”

The post Your AI coding agent now runs on a budget — and it can cut you off mid-task appeared first on The New Stack.
Cognition’s hierarchical budgets let enterprises govern Devin’s AI agent spend across teams and projects, and stop sessions when a budget runs out.

item.title: Canva’s new design model doesn’t generate images. It writes code to edit them.
item.dc:creator: Adrian Bridgwater
item.description:
Australian graphic design software company Canva took the wraps off Canva Brush last week, its new vision-language model for designers.

The post Canva’s new design model doesn’t generate images. It writes code to edit them. appeared first on The New Stack.
item.content:encoded:
Australian graphic design software company Canva took the wraps off Canva Brush last week, its new vision-language model for designers. Brush is an editing model rather than an image generator: a vision-language model that understands the intent behind a designer’s project and interprets design change requests. 

Available to Canva Pro users, Canva says Brush reads a design’s content and structure, writes and executes small pieces of code to make changes, then checks its own result. Canva Brush arrived a week after Canva’s first in-house image-generation model, Canva Craft, which launched on October 22. 

Design is complex; design editing is even more complex

According to a Canva launch blog, generating high-quality designs is one of the biggest challenges for AI models, but “editing them is even more complex” today. This is because the model needs to understand what a designer wants to change, how the design is structured, and importantly, what needs to stay exactly as it is. Otherwise, a simple edit request can result in a “whole bunch of changes” nobody asked for.

In a prompt such as, “Make me a 3-page pitch deck for my bakery with Art Nouveau visuals and backgrounds,” an agent has to make a long chain of decisions. It needs to plan a narrative across pages, generate and place text, select imagery, and keep typography, color, and spacing consistent from the first page to the last. Each decision connects to the next, and small missteps can add up to a design that’s off-brand or feels out of kilter.

“That’s exactly the challenge we’ve built Brush to solve. Rather than treating design as a series of isolated decisions, Brush can continually evaluate and improve its work, helping [users] take an idea from a rough sketch to a polished design that’s ready to share. Behind the scenes, it uses an agentic loop that writes and runs code to adjust design elements, and can then inspect what’s happening on the page to guide its next step,” stated Canva.

“Bounded problems – for well-defined, specific tasks – are where small specialized models have been quietly beating large general ones for years.”

This is not a frontier lab challenge; it’s smarter than that

The question then is: can an art- and design-focused AI model lab from down under Australia challenge the frontier model behemoths on complex image design editing tasks over the long term?

Enterprise AI architect & founder of Besk Tech, Vladimir Beskorovainyi, tells The New Stack that this question is “posed in the wrong frame” both metaphorically and literally.

“Canva is not challenging frontier models; it is in fact declining to compete with them,” Beskorovainyi says. “A model that reads how a design is assembled (and edits it) is solving a bounded problem (one with well-defined specific tasks with clear parameters and limited scope), and bounded problems are where small specialized models have been quietly beating large general ones for years.” 

Urging us to look beyond the capabilities of the Canva Brush model and focus more directly on the cost per edit, Beskorovainyi thinks that “the moat here is the artifact, not the weights”, primarily, Canva can train on how real designs are actually put together.

“A frontier lab can match the base processing capability of a tool like Canva Brush; the training signal is the harder thing to match, because it comes from holding the designs,” asserts Beskorovainyi. “Verticalization wins wherever the data is a by-product of the product rather than something you have to go and buy. That is the part most model developers still underestimate.”

Design expertise, plus anonymized insights 

Brush started by drawing from an unspecified open-weights model, which Canva then post-trained on real design and editing tasks, using a combination of design expertise and anonymized insights from people who opted in to help improve Canva AI. As a result, it understands not only what a finished result looks like, but also the steps needed to get there. 

“We combined post-training with large-scale reinforcement learning, giving the model opportunities to work through complete design and editing tasks, learn from what worked, and continually shape its future behavior,” the company notes in its announcement.

“A beautiful edit can still be an expensive proofreading assignment.”

Sensitive to designers’ real-world needs as they’re urged to put down their Rotring pens and Pantone color guides and adopt agentically driven toolsets, many in the marcoms industry have opinions on these new services.

Founder of Dr. Rissy’s Writing & Marketing, Dr. Morissa Schwartz, tells The New Stack that she has used many automation tools over the years, hasn’t yet used Canva Brush, but knows what she would do if she did.

“Here is the marketing and publishing test I would put it through. An AI design editor earns its keep when a ‘change this headline’ command still leaves the price, disclaimer, and layout intact,” Schwartz explains. “Canva’s opportunity is to make those small, frequent revisions dependable enough that a marketing team spends less time checking what else moved.”

She notes that she would further test Brush against a general-purpose model on the same approved design and measure unintended changes, legibility and time to human approval, rather than image-generation rankings. 

“A beautiful edit can still be an expensive proofreading assignment,” adds Schwartz.

“Frontier models know the Internet; Canva knows what hundreds of millions of people actually do with a slide deck. In a vertical, taste and distribution beat parameter count.”

Canva is “out-niching” the frontier labs

Co-founder and CTO of deep-tech venture studio The Capital Index, Rodion Sorokin, tells The New Stack that he agrees with the sentiment expressed thus far and says “Canva isn’t trying to out-muscle the frontier labs; it’s out-niching them” in real terms. 

“Brush started from an open-weights model and was trained with reinforcement learning against what Canva’s own designers call good design, a playbook any well-funded vertical player can now copy,” Sorokin says. “Frontier models know the Internet; Canva knows what hundreds of millions of people actually do with a slide deck. In a vertical, taste and distribution beat parameter count.”

“The clever bit is that Brush doesn’t paint pixels: it reads the layers, writes small pieces of code to change them and checks its own work, which is how a designer edits, not how an image generator guesses. Canva says that makes it up to 69% faster than its previous design agent at 46% lower cost per task. If that holds up outside a launch blog, specialized models will win on unit economics, not just quality: generation becomes the commodity, and editing becomes the business,” adds Sorokin.

AI model benchmarking platform ranking

According to Canva, Craft (not Brush) debuted as the fourth-ranked model on crowdsourced benchmarking platform Design Arena, behind OpenAI’s precision-focused image generation and editing model GPT Image 2.5 Sunburst, the speed-focused image generation model GPT Image 2.5 Flare, and GPT Image 2. Canva Research’s in-house 160-person AI lab developed both Canva Craft and the new Canva Brush models. Canva’s speed and cost figures for Brush are self-reported and compare it with the company’s previous design agent, not with frontier models.

Canva has stated that everything Canva Brush creates is fully editable. Every element, from the text and imagery to the colors, layouts, and finer details, remains available for designers to edit, manipulate, and rearrange however they like.

The organization also confirmed that this release represents the first version of Brush, and “there’s plenty more to come,” as the company is already working on the ability to reference attachments, improvements to how Brush handles image-heavy layouts, and Brand Kit support in the future.

The post Canva’s new design model doesn’t generate images. It writes code to edit them. appeared first on The New Stack.
Canva’s new Brush model edits designs by writing code, not painting pixels. Experts say that’s how a vertical player sidesteps the frontier labs.

item.title: OpenAI’s new shared usage limit pits ChatGPT against Codex
item.dc:creator: Paul Sawers
item.description:
OpenAI has revealed plans to combine usage allowances across ChatGPT and Codex, as part of a broader effort to integrate

The post OpenAI’s new shared usage limit pits ChatGPT against Codex appeared first on The New Stack.
item.content:encoded:
OpenAI has revealed plans to combine usage allowances across ChatGPT and Codex, as part of a broader effort to integrate its conversational AI and agentic capabilities into a single experience.

In a help article quietly published over the weekend, the company confirmed the changes will take effect “starting in December,” affecting Plus, Pro and Business subscribers. Under the new system, ChatGPT conversations and Codex tasks will draw from a common pool of tokens, with more demanding models and complex tasks consuming a greater share — though OpenAI has yet to disclose how generous the combined allowance will be.

Instant chat, ChatGPT’s faster-response mode for everyday questions and tasks, will be exempt.

OpenAI’s products come together

The changes are the latest step in OpenAI’s efforts to bring its growing collection of AI products under one roof.

In July, the company launched ChatGPT Work, an agentic tool built on its Codex coding technology that allows users to delegate complex tasks, such as researching topics, analysing data and producing documents, presentations and spreadsheets. The idea was to extend the capabilities of Codex beyond software development, allowing knowledge workers to use AI agents for everyday business tasks.

As The New Stack reported at the time, the launch also saw OpenAI consolidate ChatGPT and Codex into a single desktop application, with dedicated interfaces for conversations, agentic tasks and coding.

ChatGPT Work joined an expanding collection of specialised tools, including ChatGPT for Excel, which debuted in March, which later extended to Google Sheets.

It’s worth noting that these products already have overlapping usage arrangements. Currently, Codex, ChatGPT Work, ChatGPT for Excel, and Workspace Agents draw from a shared agentic allowance, while regular ChatGPT conversations have separate usage limits.

And it’s that very separation that’s set to change from December, putting developers in a position where intensive Codex sessions eat into the allowance available for ChatGPT conversations, and vice versa.

‘ChatGPT and Codex serve different purposes’

OpenAI isn’t alone in bringing its conversational and agentic products closer together. In September, Anthropic merged Claude Chat and Cowork into a single interface, allowing users to move from asking questions to delegating more involved tasks within the same conversation.

This shows how two of the biggest frontier AI labs are pursuing a similar goal: making it easier for users to switch between asking questions, and carrying out more substantial tasks, without having to navigate separate products. However, OpenAI’s decision to combine usage allowances has prompted objections from subscribers concerned that the change could leave them with less access to the tools they already pay for.

“ChatGPT and Codex serve different purposes, and their usage limits should remain separate.”

In a discussion kickstarted on OpenAI’s developer forum on Saturday, users called on the company to abandon the proposed consolidation, or guarantee that subscribers won’t end up with less usable capacity under the new system. The forum member who started the discussion, going under the moniker Smalikou, argues that the two products should retain independent allowances and called for greater transparency over how usage will be calculated.

“ChatGPT and Codex serve different purposes, and their usage limits should remain separate,” they write.

Another user, going by the name of PZA, calls for more detailed usage reporting, including a breakdown of consumption by product, model and task.

“If OpenAI decides to combine them anyway, a real-time usage dashboard must be available before the change takes effect,” they write. “It should show the remaining allowance, reset time, and consumption by product, model, and task. Without that transparency, I will consider the change a downgrade to my paid plan and reconsider renewing.”

As it happens, OpenAI has confirmed that subscribers will be able to see their combined remaining allowance and reset times in ChatGPT’s settings, but hasn’t specified what level of detail it will include.

The concerns come just days after OpenAI reversed a controversial decision to halve usage limits for its $200 Pro subscription. On October 29, the company confirmed it was cancelling the Pro 200 reduction, restoring the higher Work and Codex allowances for subscribers already moved to the lower limits, while doubling allowances for Pro 100, Pro 500 and Business Premium subscribers.

Tibo Sottiaux, OpenAI’s head of ChatGPT and Codex, acknowledged the criticism surrounding the proposed reduction, writing on X that the company had heard subscribers’ feedback and would preserve existing Pro 200 allowances.

“We heard your kind feedback and won’t be reducing usage limits for Pro 200, so your Work and Codex usage will stay the same,” he wrote.

However, one forum participant questioned how much those increases would benefit subscribers once ChatGPT conversations begin drawing from the same allowance as Codex. The user, posting as Zigg88, notes that they already regularly approach their weekly Codex limit.

“Doubling a resource allocation while simultaneously expanding the number of things consuming it doesn’t inherently translate into more usable capacity,” they write.

Others raised concerns about the impact on their ability to use ChatGPT for research and technical planning while relying on Codex for software development, with one commenter arguing that OpenAI should preserve independent allowances or guarantee equivalent access under the new system.

The New Stack reached out to OpenAI to ask when, exactly, the changes would take effect in December, and whether the new combined allowance would be equivalent to the existing separate allowances, or leave some subscribers with less usable capacity. The company declined to answer the questions, instead reiterating its recent increases to Work and Codex usage limits, and directing us to its existing documentation.

For now, OpenAI says it expects most users to encounter usage resets no more frequently than they do today. However, without publishing the new token allowances or explaining how they compare with existing limits, subscribers have little way of knowing whether that reassurance will hold true for them.
